c-us3-ov-enumeration.text: The Constitution required that 'The actual Enumeration shall be made within three Years after the first Meeting of the Congress of the United States', and then 'within every subsequent Term of ten Years'. The Census Bureau's history notes that 'Following independence, there was an almost immediate need for a census of the entire Nation.'
c-us3-ov-enumeration.label: consensus

c-us3-ov-1790.text: The first census, of 1790, counted 3,929,214 residents in 13 states, about 4.5 people per square mile. The Census Bureau estimates that it used about 650 enumerators and lists Thomas Jefferson as the official in charge.
c-us3-ov-1790.label: approx
c-us3-ov-1790.note: The total is the Bureau's official figure for an early count; the Bureau marks the number of enumerators '(est.)'.

c-us3-ov-decades.text: The census counted 5,308,483 residents in 1800 (16 states), 7,239,881 in 1810 (17), 9,638,453 in 1820 (23) and 17,063,353 in 1840 (26). The Bureau gives 6.1 people per square mile of land area in 1800, 4.3 in 1810 and 9.8 in 1840.
c-us3-ov-decades.label: consensus

c-us3-ov-1830.text: The 1830 census counted 12,860,702 residents in 24 states, 7.4 per square mile of land area; its largest urban place was New York City, with 202,589.
c-us3-ov-1830.label: consensus

c-us3-ov-1850.text: The 1850 census counted 23,191,876 residents in 30 states, 7.9 per square mile; its largest urban place was New York City, with 515,547.
c-us3-ov-1850.label: consensus

c-us3-ov-area.text: Dividing each census's population by its density gives a land area of roughly 873,000 square miles in 1790 and about 2.94 million square miles in 1850, more than three times as much.
c-us3-ov-area.label: approx
c-us3-ov-area.note: Our arithmetic from the Census Bureau's population and density figures, not a Bureau statistic.

c-us3-ov-louisiana.text: By the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, 'For roughly 4 cents an acre, the United States doubled its size, expanding the nation westward.'
c-us3-ov-louisiana.label: approx
c-us3-ov-louisiana.note: The National Archives' round figures for price per acre and area.

c-us3-ov-parties.text: American debate over the French Revolution 'exacerbated pre-existing political divisions': 'Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson became the leader of the pro-French Democratic-Republican Party', while 'Hamilton led the Federalist Party, which viewed the Revolution with skepticism'.
c-us3-ov-parties.label: consensus

c-us3-ov-annals.text: The Annals of Congress, covering 1789 to 1824, were 'compiled between 1834 and 1856, using the best records available, primarily newspaper accounts'; in them 'Speeches are paraphrased rather than presented verbatim.'
c-us3-ov-annals.label: consensus

c-us3-ov-tocqueville.text: Alexis de Tocqueville's Democracy in America appeared in two parts, in 1835 and 1840, and asked 'how to preserve liberty within a society characterized by rapidly increasing equality of conditions'. In the first part he wrote that 'nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions'.
c-us3-ov-tocqueville.label: consensus

c-us3-ov-banneker.text: In August 1791 Benjamin Banneker, a free Black American, wrote to Jefferson charging him with 'detaining by fraud and violence so numerous a part of my brethren under groaning captivity and cruel oppression'.
c-us3-ov-banneker.label: consensus

c-us3-ham-debt.text: In January 1790 Hamilton put the federal debt, foreign and domestic, at 'together 54,124,464 dollars, and 56 cents', and wrote that for the states' debts 'the total amount may be safely stated at 25 millions of dollars'.
c-us3-ham-debt.label: approx
c-us3-ham-debt.note: Hamilton's own figures; he presented the state total as an estimate, less exact than the federal one.

c-us3-ham-assume.text: Hamilton wrote of the debt that 'It was the price of liberty.', and argued that 'it is expedient, there should be an assumption of the state debts by the Union.'
c-us3-ham-assume.label: consensus

c-us3-ham-bargain.text: Jefferson later wrote an account of how assumption passed. Of Hamilton and Madison he says: 'I immediately wrote to each to come and dine with me the next day'; 'It ended in Mr. Madison's acquiescence in a proposition that the question should be again brought before the house': Madison 'would not vote for it, nor entirely withdraw his opposition, yet he should not be strenuous'. Jefferson adds that 'It was agreed to speak to Mr. White and Mr. Lee, whose districts lay on the Patowmac', that the capital would go to the Potomac, with 'an intermediate residence at Philadelphia' to win Pennsylvania, and that assumption 'was finally carried by the change of White's and Lee's votes.'
c-us3-ham-bargain.label: tradition
c-us3-ham-bargain.note: This is Jefferson's own account, written later (the editors of his papers date it '[1792?]'); it is one participant's memory, not a neutral record, and its date for the dinner is not given here.

c-us3-ham-bank.text: President Washington signed the bill for the Bank of the United States in February 1791. It started with capital of $10 million, '$2 million of which was owned by the government', and 'opened for business in Philadelphia on December 12, 1791, with a twenty-year charter'.
c-us3-ham-bank.label: consensus

c-us3-ham-bank-1811.text: In January 1811 the House voted against renewing the charter 'by just one vote'; the Senate tied, and 'The vice president, George Clinton of New York, cast the tie-breaking vote' against renewal.
c-us3-ham-bank-1811.label: consensus

c-us3-ham-necessary.text: Jefferson argued that 'the constitution allows only the means which are "necessary" not those which are merely "convenient"'; Hamilton replied that 'necessary often means no more than needful, requisite, incidental, useful, or conducive to.'
c-us3-ham-necessary.label: debated
c-us3-ham-necessary.note: In 1791 Jefferson (strict reading) and Hamilton (broad reading) gave Washington opposite advice; for the Supreme Court's later answer see US2.2.

c-us3-ham-manuf.text: Hamilton's Report on Manufactures (5 December 1791) argued that for new industries 'the interference and aid of their own government are indispensible', and that 'The seperation of occupations causes each to be carried to a much greater perfection' (original spelling).
c-us3-ham-manuf.label: consensus

c-us3-ham-whiskey.text: The whiskey excise of 1791 was 'the first national internal revenue tax'. In July 1794 about 500 armed men burned the home of the regional tax inspector in western Pennsylvania; 'Washington ordered some 13,000 troops into the area, but the opposition melted away and no battle ensued', and 'the two convicted of treason were later pardoned by the president.'
c-us3-ham-whiskey.label: approx
c-us3-ham-whiskey.note: Britannica's round figures for the rioters and the troops.

c-us3-ham-farewell.text: In his Farewell Address (19 September 1796) Washington warned of 'the baneful effects of the Spirit of Party', advised that ''Tis our true policy to steer clear of permanent Alliances', and wrote that 'Religion and morality are indispensable supports.'
c-us3-ham-farewell.label: consensus

c-us3-ham-legacy.text: Peter Rousseau and Richard Sylla argue that the financial system built in the 1790s 'was central to the nation's early growth and modernization'; Hall, Payne, Sargent and Szőke (2021) measure how long Hamilton's policy took to work 'by building a reputation for servicing debts as promised'; Terry Bouton's Taming Democracy (2007), a study of Pennsylvania, argues, in a reviewer's words, that the American gentry from 1776 to roughly 1800 succeeded at 'stunting the meaning and practice of democracy for ordinary white men.'
c-us3-ham-legacy.label: debated
c-us3-ham-legacy.note: Economic historians (Rousseau and Sylla; Hall, Payne, Sargent and Szőke, a new 2021 study) credit Hamilton's system with building national credit and growth. The historian Terry Bouton stresses the founding gentry's cost to democracy for ordinary white men; the review cited does not discuss Hamilton's programme itself.

c-us3-party-france.text: American debate over the French Revolution 'exacerbated pre-existing political divisions' and 'resulted in the alignment of the political elite along pro-French and pro-British lines': Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson led the pro-French Democratic-Republican Party, and 'Hamilton led the Federalist Party, which viewed the Revolution with skepticism'.
c-us3-party-france.label: consensus

c-us3-party-jay.text: John Jay's treaty with Britain 'was immensely unpopular with the American public', and it 'squeaked through the Senate on a 20 to 10 vote on June 24, 1795.'
c-us3-party-jay.label: consensus

c-us3-party-acts.text: In 1798 'a Federalist-controlled Congress passed four laws, known collectively as the Alien and Sedition Acts.' They 'raised the residency requirements for citizenship from 5 to 14 years', and the Sedition Act made it a crime to publish any 'false, scandalous, and malicious writing' about the government. 'The only journalists prosecuted under the Sedition Act were editors of Democratic-Republican newspapers.'
c-us3-party-acts.label: consensus

c-us3-party-sunset.text: The Sedition Act was to remain in force 'until the third day of March, one thousand eight hundred and one, and no longer'; the acts were later 'repealed or allowed to expire'.
c-us3-party-sunset.label: consensus

c-us3-party-authors.text: The Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions were 'Drafted in secret by future Presidents Thomas Jefferson and James Madison', who 'kept their authorship of the resolutions secret because they feared arrest for sedition.' They argued that 'the Union is a compact among individual states that delegates specific powers to the federal government'. Kentucky passed Jefferson's resolutions in 1798, and Virginia passed 'its more temperate resolution on Christmas Eve of the same year.'
c-us3-party-authors.label: consensus

c-us3-party-va.text: The Virginia Resolution, 'Agreed to by the Senate, December 24, 1798', declared that 'the states who are parties thereto, have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose' against unconstitutional federal acts.
c-us3-party-va.label: consensus

c-us3-party-ky.text: Kentucky's further resolution, 'Approved December 3rd, 1799', held that the states 'have the unquestionable right to judge of its infraction', and that 'a nullification, by those sovereignties, of all unauthorized acts done under colour of that instrument, is the rightful remedy'.
c-us3-party-ky.label: consensus

c-us3-party-later.text: In the nullification crisis of the early 1830s 'states' rights figures such as John Calhoun and Robert Hayne explicitly cited the Virginia and Kentucky Resolutions as early exemplifications of their theory', but Madison did not believe that a single state had the authority to nullify federal law within its own borders.
c-us3-party-later.label: debated
c-us3-party-later.note: What the resolutions meant is disputed: Calhoun and Hayne read them as precedents for nullification; Madison, as Douglas Dow (updated by John R. Vile, 2024) reports, said they were meant to shape opinion and rally other states, not to block federal law (see US3.7).

c-us3-party-1800.text: In 1800 Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied in the electoral college because electors could not indicate a presidential or vice-presidential choice; the House chose Jefferson on 17 February 1801 'after 36 ballots and with Federalists in Maryland and Vermont abstaining', and Hamilton 'tried to engineer support for Jefferson' over Burr.
c-us3-party-1800.label: consensus

c-us3-party-12th.text: The Twelfth Amendment (passed by Congress 9 December 1803, ratified 15 June 1804) requires electors to name the president and 'in distinct ballots the person voted for as Vice-President'.
c-us3-party-12th.label: consensus

c-us3-party-roane.text: In 1819 Jefferson called his election 'as real a revolution in the principles of our government as that of 76.'
c-us3-party-roane.label: consensus

c-us3-jeff-purchase.text: Jefferson sent James Monroe to join Robert Livingston in France, and in 1803 the United States bought Louisiana, which 'included 828,000 square miles', from France 'for $15 million.'
c-us3-jeff-purchase.label: approx
c-us3-jeff-purchase.note: The price is exact; the area is a modern estimate for a territory whose boundaries were not defined at the time.

c-us3-jeff-napoleon.text: Napoleon gave up his plans for Louisiana when 'the French Army in St. Domingue was being decimated by yellow fever, and war between France and England still threatened.'
c-us3-jeff-napoleon.label: consensus

c-us3-jeff-constitution.text: Jefferson wrote to John Breckinridge on 12 August 1803 that 'the constitution has made no provision for our holding foreign territory', and that the Executive had 'done an act beyond the constitution.'
c-us3-jeff-constitution.label: consensus

c-us3-jeff-miller.text: Robert J. Miller argues, in his publisher's description, that 'Thomas Jefferson used the doctrine' of Discovery 'to exert American authority in the Louisiana Territory' and to '"conquer" the Indian nations'.
c-us3-jeff-miller.label: debated
c-us3-jeff-miller.note: Miller reads the purchase through the legal Doctrine of Discovery and its claims over Native lands; the Office of the Historian and the National Archives describe it as a purchase of territory from France.

c-us3-jeff-corps.text: 'On May 14, 1804 William Clark and the Corps of Discovery left Camp River Dubois', more than 45 members strong; they reached 'the Pacific Ocean by November of 1805' and arrived in St. Louis on 23 September 1806. They included Sacagawea, the Shoshone wife of the interpreter Toussaint Charbonneau, with her newborn son Jean Baptiste, and York, 'who had been enslaved by William Clark since his childhood.'
c-us3-jeff-corps.label: consensus

c-us3-jeff-embargo.text: Douglas Irwin estimates that the embargo on international shipping, from December 1807 to March 1809, cost 'about 8 percent of America's 1807 GNP', when trade was roughly 13 percent of output; the cost was smaller because some trade continued and 'domestic producers successfully shifted production toward previously imported manufactured goods'.
c-us3-jeff-embargo.label: approx
c-us3-jeff-embargo.note: A model-based estimate from price data (Irwin, NBER 2001; Review of International Economics, 2005); there were no national accounts in 1807.

c-us3-jeff-war.text: Madison 'asked Congress for a declaration of War on Great Britain on June 1, 1812.' The causes included British efforts 'to impress American seamen on the high seas into the Royal Navy', restrictions on neutral trade, and 'western expansion, relations with American Indians, and territorial control of North America.'
c-us3-jeff-war.label: consensus

c-us3-jeff-ghent.text: 'By 1814 neither side could claim a clear victory.' The British blockaded the east coast and attacked Washington, 'burning the White House and other Government buildings'. On Christmas Eve 1814 negotiators signed the Treaty of Ghent, 'restoring the political boundaries on the North American continent to the status quo ante bellum'.
c-us3-jeff-ghent.label: consensus

c-us3-jeff-hartford.text: Federalists from Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Vermont met at Hartford from 15 December 1814 to 5 January 1815; its more extreme members 'raised the possibility of secession'. The convention proposed amendments to apportion representatives and direct taxes 'according to their respective numbers of free persons', to forbid declaring war 'without the concurrence of two-thirds of both Houses' except when the country was 'actually invaded', to bar embargoes 'for more than sixty days', and to forbid electing a president 'from the same State two terms in succession'.
c-us3-jeff-hartford.label: consensus

c-us3-jeff-threefifths.text: The Constitution apportioned House seats by adding to the free persons, 'excluding Indians not taxed, three fifths of all other Persons.'
c-us3-jeff-threefifths.label: consensus

c-us3-jeff-hartford-end.text: Even as the convention finished, 'a British sloop of war was beating its way across the Atlantic with dispatches containing the peace terms' of the Treaty of Ghent, and as its emissaries approached Washington they 'were met by the news of Gen. Andrew Jackson's unexpected victory in the Battle of New Orleans', so that 'it was no longer possible to serve the kind of ultimatum contained in the convention's report'; 'its unpopularity was a factor in the demise of the Federalist Party.'
c-us3-jeff-hartford-end.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-virginia.text: Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom, written by Jefferson in 1777, was adopted on 16 January 1786, after James Madison anonymously wrote the Memorial and Remonstrance against the General Assessment, a proposed tax to support all Christian sects that Patrick Henry championed. It provides that 'no man shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship, place, or ministry whatsoever.'
c-us3-relig-virginia.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-first.text: The First Amendment begins: 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof'.
c-us3-relig-first.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-mass.text: 'Massachusetts was the last of the original 13 states officially to disestablish its churches in 1833.'
c-us3-relig-mass.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-danbury.text: Jefferson's reply of 1 January 1802 to the Danbury Baptists spoke of 'thus building a wall of separation between Church & State.'
c-us3-relig-danbury.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-hutson.text: In 1998 the FBI made Jefferson's erased draft of the Danbury letter legible. It shows that on Levi Lincoln's advice he 'deleted the entire section about thanksgivings and fasts', which Lincoln feared 'could hurt Jefferson politically among the growing number of Republicans in New England'; 'Federalist preachers had routinely used fast and thanksgiving days to revile Jefferson and his followers.' James Hutson, chief of the Library of Congress's Manuscript Division, concludes that 'it was meant to be a political manifesto, nothing more.' The Supreme Court in Reynolds v. United States (1878) had said that Jefferson's words might 'be accepted almost as an authoritative declaration of the scope and effect of the [first] amendment.'
c-us3-relig-hutson.label: debated
c-us3-relig-hutson.note: Hutson reads the letter as a political document of 1802; the Supreme Court, from Reynolds (1878) to McCollum (1948), as Hutson reports, treated its metaphor as a statement of constitutional principle (see US2.9).

c-us3-relig-awakening.text: The Second Great Awakening, roughly 1795 to 1835, spread 'particularly among Methodist and Baptist churches' and 'stimulated several moral and philanthropic reforms, including temperance and the emancipation of women.'
c-us3-relig-awakening.label: approx
c-us3-relig-awakening.note: The start and end dates of a revival movement are conventional.

c-us3-relig-hatch.text: Nathan Hatch argues that in these decades 'American Christianity was democratized and common people became powerful actors on the religious scene.'
c-us3-relig-hatch.label: debated
c-us3-relig-hatch.note: One historian's influential interpretation, given here from the publisher's description; it is a thesis, not a measured fact, and no opposing study was consulted for this page.

c-us3-relig-caneridge.text: At the camp meeting at Cane Ridge, Bourbon County, Kentucky, on 6-12 August 1801, crowd 'estimates range from 10,000 to 30,000.'
c-us3-relig-caneridge.label: approx
c-us3-relig-caneridge.note: Nobody counted; the range is that of contemporary and later estimates.

c-us3-relig-ame.text: At St. George's church in Philadelphia 'blacks had been confined to the gallery of the church'; 'The frustration of segregation and further racial tensions led Allen and more than forty others to leave St. George's', and in 1816 Richard Allen was consecrated 'bishop of the newly organized AME Church'.
c-us3-relig-ame.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-moroni.text: According to Latter-day Saint tradition, 'an angel named Moroni told him', Joseph Smith, 'about engraved golden plates'.
c-us3-relig-moroni.label: tradition
c-us3-relig-moroni.note: The church's own account of its origins, reported by Britannica; historians record that believers hold it, not that it happened.

c-us3-relig-lds.text: The Book of Mormon was published in 1830, and the church was organized on 6 April 1830; 'Surviving firsthand accounts from attendees contradict one another on the location of the founding meeting, some reporting Fayette and others Manchester.' Joseph Smith was killed by a mob at Carthage, Illinois, on 27 June 1844.
c-us3-relig-lds.label: approx
c-us3-relig-lds.note: The date is agreed; the place is uncertain because those present remembered it differently.

c-us3-relig-touro.text: 'Dedicated in 1763, Touro Synagogue is the oldest synagogue building in the United States.'
c-us3-relig-touro.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-newport.text: On 18 August 1790 Washington wrote to the Hebrew Congregation in Newport that 'It is now no more that toleration is spoken of, as if it was by the indulgence of one class of people', praised 'the Government of the United States, which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance', and wrote of a time 'while every one shall sit in safety under his own vine and figtree, and there shall be none to make him afraid.'
c-us3-relig-newport.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-micah.text: Micah 4:4 reads, in the NRSVUE: 'but they shall all sit under their own vines and under their own fig trees, and no one shall make them afraid, for the mouth of the Lord of hosts has spoken.'
c-us3-relig-micah.label: consensus

c-us3-relig-jews.text: The Jewish population of the United States was about 3,000 in 1820; 'Between 1840 and 1860 the Jewish population of this country ballooned from 15,000 to 150,000.'
c-us3-relig-jews.label: approx
c-us3-relig-jews.note: The Library of Congress's round estimates; there was no religious census.

c-us3-relig-temperance.text: The earliest temperance organizations 'seem to have been those founded at Saratoga, New York, in 1808 and in Massachusetts in 1813'; churches had introduced an abstinence pledge 'as early as 1800', the movement 'spread rapidly under the influence of the churches', and 'by 1833 there were 6,000 local societies in several U.S. states.'
c-us3-relig-temperance.label: approx
c-us3-relig-temperance.note: Britannica's round figure for the number of societies; it also hedges on which societies came first ('seem to have been').

c-us3-relig-seneca.text: At Seneca Falls on 19 and 20 July 1848 a Declaration of Sentiments 'drafted by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and the M'Clintock family', declaring that 'all men and women are created equal', was signed by '68 women and 32 men'. 'Eleven of the resolutions proposed in the "Declaration" passed unanimously', but the suffrage resolution was 'narrowly approved', after 'Frederick Douglass stood with Stanton and argued forcefully' for it.
c-us3-relig-seneca.label: approx
c-us3-relig-seneca.note: The signer count of 68 women and 32 men is the National Park Service's; the Library of Congress gives 'signed by 100 individuals, 62 women and 38 men.'

c-us3-mkt-fulton.text: Robert Fulton's steamboat ran 150 miles up the Hudson from New York to Albany in August 1807; the trip took 32 hours.
c-us3-mkt-fulton.label: consensus

c-us3-mkt-erie.text: Work on the Erie Canal began in 1817 and it was completed in 1825; it ran 363 miles, and New York State authorized loans of $7 million to build it.
c-us3-mkt-erie.label: consensus

c-us3-mkt-erie-freight.text: After the Erie Canal opened, freight rates from upstate New York to the Atlantic fell by about 90 percent, and hauling time fell from 30 days to 10.
c-us3-mkt-erie-freight.label: approx
c-us3-mkt-erie-freight.note: Round figures, quoted by JSTOR Daily (2025) from the historian Justin Nordstrom.

c-us3-mkt-rail.text: About 3,000 miles of railroad track had been laid in the United States by 1840, and about 30,000 miles by 1860.
c-us3-mkt-rail.label: approx
c-us3-mkt-rail.note: Rounded totals compiled by Jean-Paul Rodrigue from Rand McNally (1898) and Poor's Manual.

c-us3-mkt-taylor.text: George Rogers Taylor's The Transportation Revolution, 1815-1860 (1951) remains a standard work; in 1977 Harry Scheiber and Stephen Salsbury made 'the case for the permanent impact' of the book.
c-us3-mkt-taylor.label: consensus

c-us3-mkt-lowell.text: The Merrimack Manufacturing Company was incorporated in 1822 and 'produces its first textiles' in 1823; Osher calls it 'the first textile manufacturing concern to open in Lowell' and says 'It was funded and planned by the Boston Associates', a group of Boston financiers who incorporated Lowell in 1826; the town had 18,000 people by 1836 and 30,000 by 1850, and its cotton came from the South, 'picked and processed by enslaved men and women'.
c-us3-mkt-lowell.label: consensus
c-us3-mkt-lowell.note: Osher's exhibition gives both 1823 and 1824 as the start.

c-us3-mkt-strikes.text: Lowell's mill women walked out in 1834, when 800 women left work to protest a 12.5 percent wage cut, and again in 1836, when 'anywhere from 1500-2000 workers turned out'.
c-us3-mkt-strikes.label: approx
c-us3-mkt-strikes.note: The National Park Service gives a range for the 1836 turnout.

c-us3-mkt-lowell-slavery.text: Lowell National Historical Park, citing Edward Baptist, says that the cotton used by the Merrimack company 'took slaves a combined 100,000 days of labor per year to produce'.
c-us3-mkt-lowell-slavery.label: approx
c-us3-mkt-lowell-slavery.note: An estimate attributed to Edward Baptist, presented in the park's Lowell Talks podcast (2021).

c-us3-mkt-bank2.text: Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States in April 1816 with a capital of $35 million, and the Bank opened in January 1817.
c-us3-mkt-bank2.label: consensus

c-us3-mkt-1819.text: In the account of the New York Fed economists James Narron, David Skeie and Donald Morgan (2014), farmers and speculators bid up land prices on easy credit from lightly regulated state banks, which the Second Bank did little to restrain and even fed in its western branches; U.S. cotton prices 'plummeted in January 1819 after British investors substituted to Indian cotton'; and the Bank's deflationary tightening brought falling prices and collapsing land values. Federal Reserve History says the Bank's cuts in credit caused 'a financial panic that drove the economy into a steep recession'.
c-us3-mkt-1819.label: consensus

c-us3-mkt-sellers.text: Charles Sellers, in The Market Revolution (1991), his most widely debated book, described a shift 'from an agrarian to a capitalist society' that carried real costs.
c-us3-mkt-sellers.label: debated
c-us3-mkt-sellers.note: Sellers's thesis is challenged by Daniel Walker Howe (2007), who dates the change earlier and judges it less harmful, as Jill Lepore's review explains.

c-us3-mkt-howe.text: Daniel Walker Howe, in What Hath God Wrought (2007), dates the change earlier than Sellers, judges it less harmful and argues that 'most American family farmers welcomed the chance to buy and sell in larger markets'; he 'refuses to use the term "market revolution"' and speaks instead of a 'communications revolution'.
c-us3-mkt-howe.label: debated
c-us3-mkt-howe.note: Howe writes against Charles Sellers (1991); Lepore's review sets out both positions.

c-us3-mkt-feller.text: Daniel Feller warned that 'a monograph that presupposes a market revolution will certainly discover one'.
c-us3-mkt-feller.label: debated
c-us3-mkt-feller.note: A caution against Sellers's framework, quoted in Jill Lepore's review of Howe.

c-us3-slav-1808.text: Jefferson signed the act banning the import of enslaved people on 2 March 1807; it took effect 'from and after the first day of January' 1808 and 'imposed heavy penalties on international traders, but did not end slavery itself or the domestic sale of slaves.' It did regulate shipping along the coast: vessels 'of less burthen than forty tons' could not carry enslaved people along the coast for sale, and larger vessels had to carry 'duplicate manifests'.
c-us3-slav-1808.label: consensus

c-us3-slav-domestic.text: In the seven decades between the ratification of the Constitution and the Civil War, about one million enslaved people were moved from the Upper South to the Lower South, roughly two-thirds of them through the domestic slave trade.
c-us3-slav-domestic.label: approx
c-us3-slav-domestic.note: Henry Louis Gates Jr., drawing on Walter Johnson. The split between people sold and people taken by migrating owners is an estimate.

c-us3-slav-cotton.text: U.S. cotton output rose from 3,135 bales in 1790 to 73,145 in 1800, 177,638 in 1810, 334,378 in 1820 and 731,452 in 1830 (L. C. Gray's figures), and to about 2 million bales a year by the mid-1840s, about 3 million by the mid-1850s and about 4 million on the eve of the Civil War (Fogel and Engerman's figures).
c-us3-slav-cotton.label: approx
c-us3-slav-cotton.note: Two series: Gray's annual figures to 1830, and rounded later figures from Fogel and Engerman (1974) as charted by Henretta.

c-us3-slav-baptist.text: Edward Baptist, in The Half Has Never Been Told (2014), argues that violence drove the rise in enslaved people's productivity: 'Violence, Baptist contends, explains the remarkable increase of labor productivity'.
c-us3-slav-baptist.label: debated
c-us3-slav-baptist.note: Eric Foner's summary. Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode (2008, 2018) reject the argument and credit new cotton varieties.

c-us3-slav-beckert.text: Sven Beckert coined the term 'war capitalism' 'to convey the inherent violence of early cotton capitalism'; in a University of Cape Town news report of 2014, 'Beckert argued that cotton exemplifies how early forms of capitalism depended not on free wage labour, but on slavery and other unfree forms of labour.'
c-us3-slav-beckert.label: debated
c-us3-slav-beckert.note: The report's summary of Beckert's argument, not his own words. Criticised, with Baptist and Walter Johnson, by Olmstead and Rhode (2018).

c-us3-slav-olmstead.text: Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode (2018) write of Baptist, Beckert and Walter Johnson that 'All three authors mishandle historical evidence and mis-characterize important events'; their earlier work (2008) found that cotton picking rates 'increased about fourfold between 1801 and 1862', driven by 'new cotton varieties'.
c-us3-slav-olmstead.label: debated
c-us3-slav-olmstead.note: The economic historians' case against the 'new history of capitalism' of Baptist, Beckert and Johnson.

c-us3-slav-turner.text: On the night of 21-22 August 1831, in Southampton County, Virginia, Nat Turner's rebels killed 'fifty-five white men, women, and children'; white people then killed 'roughly three dozen Black people without trials', and Turner was executed on 11 November 1831.
c-us3-slav-turner.label: approx
c-us3-slav-turner.note: Encyclopedia Virginia's figures; the number killed without trial is an estimate.

c-us3-slav-virginia.text: After the revolt the Virginia legislature judged ending slavery 'inexpedient' and passed restrictions 'aimed at further suppressing Black religion and limiting the rights of free Blacks'.
c-us3-slav-virginia.label: consensus

c-us3-slav-allen.text: Richard Allen built Bethel church in Philadelphia, and in 1816 he 'united other African Methodist congregations' into the African Methodist Episcopal Church and became its bishop.
c-us3-slav-allen.label: consensus

c-us3-slav-garrison.text: William Lloyd Garrison's The Liberator first appeared on 1 January 1831, declaring 'I am in earnest', and that its editor would 'not equivocate', would 'not retreat a single inch' and would 'be heard'.
c-us3-slav-garrison.label: consensus

c-us3-slav-douglass.text: Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery on 3 September 1838, 'dressed as a sailor', and in 1845 published his first autobiography.
c-us3-slav-douglass.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-suffrage.text: In the Jacksonian era 'Suffrage was expanded as property and other restrictions on voting were reduced or abandoned in most states.'
c-us3-jack-suffrage.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-ny1821.text: New York's constitution of 1821 dropped the property test for white men but required 'm[e]n of colour' to own a freehold worth $250; in 1825 only 298 of nearly 6,000 free adult Black New Yorkers qualified.
c-us3-jack-ny1821.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-pa1838.text: In 1838 Pennsylvania restricted the vote 'to "white freemen" only'.
c-us3-jack-pa1838.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-1828.text: In 1828 Andrew Jackson won 642,553 popular votes (56 percent) to John Quincy Adams's 500,897 (43.6 percent), and 178 electoral votes to 83; in South Carolina and Delaware the legislatures chose the electors.
c-us3-jack-1828.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-turnout.text: By the American Presidency Project's figures, turnout in presidential elections was 57.6 percent in 1828, 55.4 in 1832, 57.8 in 1836, 80.2 in 1840, 78.9 in 1844 and 72.7 in 1848. The Project heads the column '% VAP', but says that 'Before 1920 the numbers used are always adjusted for the shifting definition of citizens with voting rights. So women are excluded before 1920.'
c-us3-jack-turnout.label: approx
c-us3-jack-turnout.note: Estimates of turnout among those entitled to vote, not shares of all adults. The Project notes that Walter Dean Burnham, the classic source for the nineteenth century, 'published only the turnout ratio, not his actual estimate of the voting age population', so the base behind the figures cannot be checked.

c-us3-jack-veto.text: In his veto of the Bank's recharter on 10 July 1832 Jackson wrote: 'It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes.'
c-us3-jack-veto.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-deposits.text: In 1833 Jackson ordered the federal deposits removed from the Second Bank, and its federal charter ended in 1836.
c-us3-jack-deposits.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-1837.text: The causes of the Panic of 1837 are debated: Peter Temin (1969) argued that the boom before it 'did not have its origins in the Bank Wars' and pointed to Mexican silver and 'the money-tightening policies of the Bank of England'; Peter Rousseau (2002) blames domestic policy, the Treasury's transfers of government balances between banks and 'a policy-induced increase in the demand for coin in the Western states'.
c-us3-jack-1837.label: debated
c-us3-jack-1837.note: Temin, as summarised by Richard Sylla, puts the cause abroad; Rousseau puts it in Jacksonian policy at home.

c-us3-jack-nullify.text: On 24 November 1832 a South Carolina convention at Columbia declared the tariff acts of 1828 and 1832 'null, void, and no law, nor binding upon this State, its officers or citizens'; Jackson's proclamation of 10 December 1832 answered that 'disunion, by armed force, is TREASON'.
c-us3-jack-nullify.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-compromise.text: Jackson signed the Compromise Tariff and the Force Bill on 2 March 1833; South Carolina then rescinded its nullification of the tariffs and nullified the Force Bill.
c-us3-jack-compromise.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-whigs.text: The Whig party was 'formally organized in 1834' in opposition to 'King Andrew', favoured 'a protective tariff and federally financed internal improvements', and in 1840 elected William Henry Harrison president.
c-us3-jack-whigs.label: consensus

c-us3-jack-legacy.text: Historians disagree about Jacksonian democracy: Arthur Schlesinger Jr. (1945) saw an effort to 'control the power of the capitalist groups'; Edward Pessen saw democratic rhetoric that hid inequality; Daniel Walker Howe calls the Jacksonians champions of white male supremacy; Robert Remini called Jackson a genuine 'man of the people'.
c-us3-jack-legacy.label: debated
c-us3-jack-legacy.note: As summarised in McGraw-Hill's 'Where Historians Disagree'. Schlesinger and Remini are broadly admiring; Pessen and Howe are critical.

c-us3-jack-feller.text: Daniel Feller notes that Schlesinger's book gave Indian affairs two sentences: 'Indian removal simply didn't seem that important to [Schlesinger].'
c-us3-jack-feller.label: debated
c-us3-jack-feller.note: Feller's point is that older admiring accounts left removal out; see US3.8.

c-us3-remov-act.text: Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act on 28 May 1830. It 'authorized the President to negotiate removal treaties with Indian tribes living east of the Mississippi River'.
c-us3-remov-act.label: consensus

c-us3-remov-message.text: In his message to Congress of 6 December 1830 Jackson presented removal as part of 'the benevolent policy of the Government'.
c-us3-remov-message.label: consensus

c-us3-remov-totals.text: By the end of Jackson's presidency almost 70 removal treaties had been signed, nearly 50,000 eastern Indians had been relocated to Indian Territory, and 25 million acres had been opened to white settlement.
c-us3-remov-totals.label: approx
c-us3-remov-totals.note: The National Archives' figures. Claudio Saunt (2020) counts 80,000 people deported by removal as a whole.

c-us3-remov-womankiller.text: In 1829 the Cherokee elder Womankiller supported the Cherokee law making unauthorised sales of land punishable by death: 'It is a good law -- it will not kill the innocent but the guilty.'
c-us3-remov-womankiller.label: consensus

c-us3-remov-worcester.text: In Worcester v. Georgia, decided on 3 March 1832, Chief Justice Marshall wrote: 'The Cherokee nation, then, is a distinct community occupying its own territory, with boundaries accurately described, in which the laws of Georgia can have no force'.
c-us3-remov-worcester.label: consensus

c-us3-remov-quip.text: Jackson is often said to have answered the ruling with the words 'John Marshall has made his decision', and so on.
c-us3-remov-quip.label: tradition
c-us3-remov-quip.note: Daniel Feller calls the attribution 'dubious at best'.

c-us3-remov-echota.text: A 'small, rump faction' of the Cherokee signed the Treaty of New Echota in late 1835, and the U.S. Senate ratified it in May 1836.
c-us3-remov-echota.label: consensus

c-us3-remov-ross.text: In 1836 the Cherokee principal chief John Ross told the U.S. Senate: 'Our cause is your own. It is the cause of liberty and justice.'
c-us3-remov-ross.label: consensus

c-us3-remov-trail.text: Cherokee removal began in May 1838 and was completed by the end of March 1839; more than 16,000 Cherokee were forcibly evicted from their homelands and sent to Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma.
c-us3-remov-trail.label: consensus

c-us3-remov-deaths.text: Estimates of Cherokee deaths differ: the National Park Service says 'More than a thousand Cherokee' died on the journey and 'perhaps several thousand' more from its consequences; the National Archives says 'Approximately 4,000 of 16,000 Cherokees died along the way'; a 2017 blog post of the National Museum of the American Indian says that 'Approximately one-fourth' of 'more than 20,000' removed died on the Trail of Tears.
c-us3-remov-deaths.label: approx
c-us3-remov-deaths.note: No count was kept; the three institutions also start from different numbers removed (16,000 or more than 20,000).

c-us3-remov-seminole.text: The Seminole Wars were fought in 1817-18, 1835-42 and 1855-58. The first began over attempts by U.S. authorities to recapture 'runaway Black slaves living among Seminole bands'; the second followed the refusal of most Seminoles to abandon their reservation, and the Seminole Nation Museum dates its start to 'Dade's Massacre in December 1835'.
c-us3-remov-seminole.label: consensus

c-us3-remov-seminole-cost.text: For the Second Seminole War, Britannica gives a cost of 'between $40,000,000 and $60,000,000' and as many as 2,000 U.S. soldiers killed; the Seminole Nation Museum gives 'an estimated fifteen million dollars' and more than 1,500 soldiers killed. By 1842 'roughly 3,000 Seminoles had been removed to the Indian Territory'; the museum counts about 3,500 Seminoles in Florida today, descended from those who stayed or returned.
c-us3-remov-seminole-cost.label: approx
c-us3-remov-seminole-cost.note: The two sources disagree on the cost by a factor of three or more, and on the soldiers' deaths.

c-us3-remov-prucha.text: Francis Paul Prucha (1969) rejected a 'devil theory' of removal: 'To call Jackson an Indian-hater... is to speak in terms that had little meaning to Jackson'; 'To Jackson this seemed the only answer.'
c-us3-remov-prucha.label: debated
c-us3-remov-prucha.note: Prucha defends Jackson's motives; Claudio Saunt (2020) and Jeffrey Ostler (2020) reject that reading.

c-us3-remov-saunt.text: Claudio Saunt (2020) argues that removal 'was not an inevitable chapter' but 'a fiercely contested political act designed to secure new lands for the expansion of slavery', which deported '80,000 men, women and children'.
c-us3-remov-saunt.label: debated
c-us3-remov-saunt.note: Saunt's thesis, as his publisher states it, against Prucha's view that Jackson saw no other answer.

c-us3-remov-genocide.text: In his paper 'Andrew Jackson in the Age of Trump', the centrepiece of the Society for Historians of the Early American Republic's 2020 plenary session, Daniel Feller dismissed the view that removal was 'deliberately vicious and inhuman, if not overtly genocidal'. In The Panorama, the society's blog, Jeffrey Ostler replied that the United States 'bears responsibility for this and other genocidal policies'. In Ostler's summary, Theda Perdue and Michael Green call removal 'ethnic cleansing', and Gary Clayton Anderson argues that it was 'ethnic cleansing and explicitly not genocide'; his publisher says that he 'uses ethnic cleansing as an analytical tool to challenge the alluring idea that Anglo-American colonialism in the New World constituted genocide.'
c-us3-remov-genocide.label: debated
c-us3-remov-genocide.note: New in 2020; the label remains contested, with Ostler on one side and Feller and Anderson on the other.

c-us3-monroe-florida.text: In 1818, in a raid against the Seminoles and escaped slaves, Andrew Jackson 'seized the Spanish forts at Pensacola and St. Marks'. Under the treaty of 1819 Spain gave up East Florida and renounced its claim to West Florida, the United States took on liability for '$5 million in damage done by American citizens who rebelled against Spain', Spain gave up its claims to the Pacific Northwest, the United States recognised Spanish sovereignty over Texas, and the treaty was ratified in 1821.
c-us3-monroe-florida.label: consensus

c-us3-monroe-treaty.text: The Adams-Onís (Transcontinental) Treaty was signed at Washington on 22 February 1819; its Article II reads: 'His Catholic Majesty cedes to the United States, in full property and sovereignty, all the territories which belong to him, situated to the eastward of the Mississippi, known by the name of East and West Florida.'
c-us3-monroe-treaty.label: consensus

c-us3-monroe-1822.text: On 8 March 1822 Monroe told Congress that 'the Provinces which have declared their independence and are in the enjoyment of it ought to be recognized'.
c-us3-monroe-1822.label: consensus

c-us3-monroe-canning.text: In letters to the U.S. minister Richard Rush dated 20 and 23 August 1823, the British foreign minister George Canning proposed that the two governments declare their shared views 'in the face of the world', but Secretary of State John Quincy Adams 'vigorously opposed cooperation with Great Britain'. The doctrine's main concepts were 'separate spheres of influence for the Americas and Europe, non-colonization, and non-intervention', and only 'In the late 1800s' did U.S. economic and military power enable it to enforce the doctrine.
c-us3-monroe-canning.label: consensus

c-us3-monroe-text.text: In his message to Congress of 2 December 1823 Monroe declared that the American continents 'are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers'; that the United States would consider any attempt by the European powers 'to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to our peace and safety'; and that 'With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere.'
c-us3-monroe-text.label: consensus

c-us3-monroe-bolivar.text: In a letter of August 1829 to Colonel Patrick Campbell, the British chargé d'affaires, Simón Bolívar, who distrusted the United States, wrote that it seemed 'destined to plague America with miseries in the name of Freedom'.
c-us3-monroe-bolivar.label: consensus

c-us3-monroe-roosevelt.text: The Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 envisioned the United States as 'an international police power' in the hemisphere; the Office of the Historian says it 'inverted the original meaning of the doctrine' and came to justify unilateral U.S. intervention in Latin America.
c-us3-monroe-roosevelt.label: debated
c-us3-monroe-roosevelt.note: The Office of the Historian sees a reversal in 1904; Jay Sexton, as Kirkus summarises him, sees in the doctrine itself a fusion of anti-colonialism and interventionism.

c-us3-monroe-sexton.text: Kirkus's review of Jay Sexton's The Monroe Doctrine (2011) reports that 'Sexton claims' Monroe's message came across as ambiguous, 'a fusion of anti-colonialism and interventionism'.
c-us3-monroe-sexton.label: debated
c-us3-monroe-sexton.note: The phrase is the reviewer's summary of Sexton's argument, not his own words; compare the Office of the Historian's view that the Roosevelt Corollary 'inverted' the doctrine.

c-us3-monroe-kerry.text: On 18 November 2013 Secretary of State John Kerry told the Organization of American States: 'The era of the Monroe Doctrine is over.'
c-us3-monroe-kerry.label: consensus

c-us3-monroe-2025.text: The National Security Strategy that the White House released in early December 2025 (Reuters reported it on 5 December) says the United States 'will reassert and enforce the Monroe Doctrine to restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere' and calls its approach a 'Trump Corollary' to the doctrine; Global News reports that the corollary prioritises American-led cooperative efforts against mass migration, drug trafficking and 'hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets'.
c-us3-monroe-2025.label: consensus

c-us3-monroe-2025-views.text: Reactions to the 'Trump Corollary' divided: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said 'Past administrations perpetuated the belief that the Monroe Doctrine had expired. They were wrong'; the University of British Columbia political scientist Max Cameron said that recent U.S. military operations in the region had created 'a sense of horror in many places that this is a return to gunboat diplomacy'.
c-us3-monroe-2025-views.label: debated
c-us3-monroe-2025-views.note: Reported by Global News, 8 December 2025; Cameron was speaking of the strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean and the buildup near Venezuela. Supporters present the corollary as a restoration of U.S. power in the hemisphere; critics compare it to gunboat diplomacy.

c-us3-mex-1830.text: Mexico's Law of April 6, 1830 tried to stop Anglo-American immigration into Texas and further imports of slaves, but in the Handbook of Texas's words it 'only slowed immigration and the Peculiar Institution, but did not curb them.'
c-us3-mex-1830.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-pop1834.text: In 1834 the non-Indian population of Texas was about 21,000, by Almonte's estimate.
c-us3-mex-pop1834.label: approx
c-us3-mex-pop1834.note: A contemporary estimate, as reported by the Handbook of Texas.

c-us3-mex-causes.text: The Handbook of Texas records that 'A new Centralist government, Siete Leyes, replaced the Constitution of 1824', and that 'Slavery has also been cited as an underlying cause of the revolution due to slaveowners' concern with protecting their peculiar institution.'
c-us3-mex-causes.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-1836.text: Texas declared independence on 2 March 1836, and its constitution guaranteed the protection of slavery; the Alamo fell on 6 March.
c-us3-mex-1836.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-goliad-sj.text: About 350 prisoners were killed at Goliad on 27 March 1836. At San Jacinto on 21 April the battle lasted only eighteen minutes, and the Mexican army lost 630 dead and 730 captured.
c-us3-mex-goliad-sj.label: approx
c-us3-mex-goliad-sj.note: Figures as given by the Handbook of Texas; numbers killed and captured are estimates.

c-us3-mex-annex.text: Congress passed the annexation resolution on 28 February 1845, and Texas legally entered the Union on 29 December 1845; antislavery sentiment was the chief obstacle to annexation.
c-us3-mex-annex.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-border.text: Mexico held that Texas ended at the Nueces River, the United States that it ran to the Rio Grande; Slidell was sent to Mexico to negotiate the purchase of the disputed areas.
c-us3-mex-border.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-osullivan.text: An unsigned editorial in the Democratic Review of July-August 1845 spoke of 'our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence', and said of the annexation of Texas: 'Slavery had nothing to do with it.' 'It is widely presumed that O'Sullivan authored this unsigned editorial'; Linda Hudson (1999) argues from textual analysis that Jane McManus Storm Cazneau, 'rather than John L. O'Sullivan, coined the term'.
c-us3-mex-osullivan.label: approx
c-us3-mex-osullivan.note: The words are certain; the author is not. Teaching American History follows the usual attribution to the editor, John L. O'Sullivan; Hudson's dissertation credits Cazneau.

c-us3-mex-manifest.text: Harvard University Press describes Reginald Horsman's Race and Manifest Destiny (1981) as showing that 'it was the merging of the Anglo-Saxon rhetoric with the experience of Americans conquering a continent that created a racialist philosophy', and that 'the belief in white American superiority was firmly ensconced in the nation's ideology by 1850'. In his foreword to the 1995 edition of Frederick Merk's Manifest Destiny and Mission (1963), John Mack Faragher writes that 'Frederick Merk rejected inevitability in favor of a more contingent interpretation of American expansionism in the 1840s.'
c-us3-mex-manifest.label: debated
c-us3-mex-manifest.note: Horsman reads Manifest Destiny as an expression of racial Anglo-Saxonism; Merk stressed that expansion was contingent, not inevitable. Horsman is given from his publisher's description, and Merk from Faragher's foreword, not from the books themselves.

c-us3-mex-war1846.text: The first major battle, Palo Alto, was fought on 8 May 1846 and Resaca de la Palma on 9 May; on 13 May 1846 the United States declared war on Mexico.
c-us3-mex-war1846.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-justwar.text: Historians still disagree about whether Polk's war was justified.
c-us3-mex-justwar.label: debated
c-us3-mex-justwar.note: Amy S. Greenberg (A Wicked War, 2012), as her Kirkus reviewer summarizes the book, presents a war waged against an unoffending neighbor. A review of Robert W. Merry (A Country of Vast Designs, 2009) sums up his verdict on Polk: 'in the end he succeeded and fulfilled the vision and dream of his constituency.'

c-us3-mex-spot.text: On 22 December 1847 Abraham Lincoln, in his Spot Resolutions, asked 'Whether the spot on which the blood of our citizens was shed, as in his messages declared,' was really American soil. The House never acted on them.
c-us3-mex-spot.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-thoreau.text: Henry David Thoreau spent a night in jail for not paying his poll tax, because he could not support a government that endorsed slavery and waged an imperialist war against Mexico; his essay 'Resistance to Civil Government' (May 1849) was later called 'Civil Disobedience'.
c-us3-mex-thoreau.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-douglass.text: In The North Star in February 1848 Frederick Douglass wrote: 'Slavery, treachery and mad ambition, are at the head of the government, in the person of James K. Polk'.
c-us3-mex-douglass.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-treaty.text: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848, made the Rio Grande the border. Mexico ceded 55 percent of its territory; the United States paid 'the sum of fifteen millions of dollars' and took over claims against Mexico 'not exceeding three and one-quarter millions of dollars'.
c-us3-mex-treaty.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-area.text: The ceded lands covered more than 500,000 square miles.
c-us3-mex-area.label: approx

c-us3-mex-citizens.text: Under Articles VIII and IX Mexicans in the ceded lands could stay or leave, keeping their property. Those who stayed could 'retain the title and rights of Mexican citizens' by declaring so within one year; the rest 'shall be incorporated into the Union of the United States', to be admitted to the rights of citizens when Congress judged proper, with their liberty, property and religion protected in the meantime.
c-us3-mex-citizens.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-senate.text: The Senate approved the treaty, with amendments, on 10 March 1848. Its Article IX 'was a new text, adapted from Article 3 of the Treaty for the Cession of Louisiana', and 'Article 10, as signed, was wholly stricken from the treaty'; that article guaranteed the protection of Mexican land grants.
c-us3-mex-senate.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-senate-vote.text: The vote to ratify, on 10 March 1848, was 38 to 14.
c-us3-mex-senate-vote.label: approx
c-us3-mex-senate-vote.note: Voteview's roll call RS0300064 and the Office of the Historian give 38 to 14. Two National Archives pages (Milestone Documents and Educator Resources) give 34 to 14.

c-us3-mex-otherside.text: Mexican writers, among them Alcaraz, Payno and Ramírez, wrote a history of the war, translated into English as The Other Side (1850), which concluded that 'the insatiable ambition of the United States, favored by our weakness, caused it.'
c-us3-mex-otherside.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-names.text: In Mexico the war is called the Guerra de 1847 or the Guerra de Estados Unidos a México. 'In Mexico, the loss of battles and territories was a national trauma', and the country 'descended into a long period of turmoil, civil war, and foreign intervention.'
c-us3-mex-names.label: consensus

c-us3-mex-whylost.label: debated
c-us3-mex-whylost.note: Peter Guardino (The Dead March, 2017), in his reviewer's summary, finds that 'Mexicans often overcame political and regional divisions and united' and that 'economics is the overriding explanation'. Brian DeLay (War of a Thousand Deserts, 2008) argues that raids by Native warriors had left northern Mexico 'too divided, exhausted, and distracted to resist'.

c-us3-mex-losses.text: Of 78,718 Americans who served in the war, 1,733 died in battle, 11,550 died of other causes in the theater of war, and 4,152 were wounded.
c-us3-mex-losses.label: approx
c-us3-mex-losses.note: Department of Veterans Affairs figures. No verified Mexican total is given on this page.

c-us3-immig-decades.text: Recorded arrivals in the United States rose from 128,502 in the 1820s to 538,381 in the 1830s, 1,427,337 in the 1840s and 2,814,554 in the 1850s.
c-us3-immig-decades.label: approx
c-us3-immig-decades.note: Official series from the DHS Yearbook, Table 2; nineteenth-century counts of arrivals are approximate.

c-us3-immig-origins.text: Ireland supplied 656,145 arrivals in the 1840s and 1,029,486 in the 1850s; Germany supplied 124,726 in the 1830s, 385,434 in the 1840s and 976,072 in the 1850s.
c-us3-immig-origins.label: approx
c-us3-immig-origins.note: DHS Yearbook, Table 2; approximate, like the totals.

c-us3-immig-blight.text: Ireland's Great Famine (1845-49, or to 1851 by some reckonings) followed crop failures caused by late blight, Phytophthora infestans.
c-us3-immig-blight.label: consensus

c-us3-immig-famine-toll.text: About 1 million people died in the Famine through starvation and disease, and over 1 million left Ireland through emigration.
c-us3-immig-famine-toll.label: approx
c-us3-immig-famine-toll.note: Round figures from the National Museum of Ireland.

c-us3-immig-cities.text: New York had 123,706 people in 1820, 312,710 in 1840 and 515,547 in 1850; Baltimore 62,738, 102,313 and 169,054; Boston 43,298, 93,383 and 136,881; New Orleans 27,176, 102,193 and 116,375. Cincinnati had 9,642 in 1820, 46,338 in 1840 and 115,435 in 1850; St. Louis, not among the 61 places in the 1820 table, had 16,469 in 1840 and 77,860 in 1850.
c-us3-immig-cities.label: consensus

c-us3-immig-phila.text: In May and July 1844 Philadelphia saw 'some of the bloodiest rioting of the antebellum period', which grew out of Catholic objections to Protestant (King James) Bible reading in the public schools; rioters burned St. Michael's and St. Augustine's Catholic churches.
c-us3-immig-phila.label: consensus

c-us3-immig-knownothing.text: In 1849 the secret Order of the Star-Spangled Banner formed in New York City. It grew into the anti-Catholic, anti-immigrant Know-Nothing movement, and by late 1855, 43 members of the House were avowed members.
c-us3-immig-knownothing.label: consensus

c-us3-immig-gold.text: On 24 January 1848 James W. Marshall found flakes of gold in the tailrace of Sutter's sawmill on the South Fork of the American River, at Coloma, in the valley the Nisenan called Cullumah ('beautiful valley').
c-us3-immig-gold.label: consensus

c-us3-immig-49ers.text: Within a year about 80,000 'forty-niners' had arrived in California.
c-us3-immig-49ers.label: approx

c-us3-immig-calpop.text: Between 1846 and 1873 California's Indian population fell from perhaps 150,000 to 30,000.
c-us3-immig-calpop.label: approx
c-us3-immig-calpop.note: The starting figure is an estimate ('perhaps 150,000').

c-us3-immig-genocide.text: Benjamin Madley (An American Genocide) argues that the killing of California's Indians in these years was genocide, and, in Newsweek's report, estimates that 'between 9,000 and 16,000 Indians, though probably many more, were killed'; Gary Clayton Anderson calls it 'ethnic cleansing, not genocide' and puts the number killed at 'no more than 2,000'.
c-us3-immig-genocide.label: debated
c-us3-immig-genocide.note: The UCLA American Indian Studies Center describes the book as 'a comprehensive and chilling history of an American genocide', and Newsweek (2016) gives his estimate of 9,000 to 16,000 Indians killed between 1846 and 1873. Gary Clayton Anderson of the University of Oklahoma told Newsweek that the term should be ethnic cleansing, not genocide, and estimated that no more than 2,000 were killed in California; Madley replied that he had 'no idea where he got that number'.

c-us3-court-dartmouth.text: In Dartmouth College v. Woodward (1819) the Court held that the college's charter of 1769 was a contract, which New Hampshire could not alter, because Article I, Section 10 forbids states to impair the obligation of contracts. Marshall wrote: 'this is a contract the obligation of which cannot be impaired without violating the Constitution'.
c-us3-court-dartmouth.label: consensus

c-us3-court-corporation.text: In the same opinion Marshall wrote: 'A corporation is an artificial being, invisible, intangible, and existing only in contemplation of law.'
c-us3-court-corporation.label: consensus

c-us3-court-webster.text: Daniel Webster argued for the college's trustees, and the decision had far-reaching impact in its application to business charters.
c-us3-court-webster.label: consensus

c-us3-court-cohens.text: In Cohens v. Virginia (1821) the Court reaffirmed that, under Section 25 of the Judiciary Act, it could review state-court judgments that raised federal questions, since 'a case arising under the Constitution or laws of the United States is cognizable in the Courts of the Union'. The opinion observed that 'In many States, the judges are dependent for office and for salary on the will of the legislature.' The Cohens' conviction stood.
c-us3-court-cohens.label: consensus

c-us3-court-crb.text: In Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge, decided on 14 February 1837, the Court held that a Massachusetts bridge charter of 1785 did not bar a rival bridge chartered in 1828, because, in the words of the case as printed in the United States Reports, 'in grants by the public, nothing passes by implication'; the same report says that 'The object and the end of all Government is to promote the happiness and prosperity of the community', and adds that 'we must not forget, that the community also have rights'.
c-us3-court-crb.label: consensus

c-us3-court-taney.text: Roger B. Taney succeeded Marshall as Chief Justice. The Supreme Court Historical Society judges that 'He interpreted corporation charters more strictly, state powers more generously, than Marshall had.'
c-us3-court-taney.label: consensus

c-us3-court-taney-rep.text: Taney's reputation has been contested from the start.
c-us3-court-taney-rep.label: debated
c-us3-court-taney-rep.note: At his appointment a New York journal wrote that the Court was 'sullied by the appointment of that political hack, Roger B. Taney'. Edward Bates, Lincoln's Attorney General, hoped that Taney's 'great error' in the Dred Scott case would not forever 'tarnish his otherwise well earned fame'.

c-us3-court-revolt.text: Two Spanish planters, Pedro Montes and José Ruiz, bought 53 Africans and put them aboard the Cuban schooner Amistad. On the night of 1-2 July 1839 the Africans, led by Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué), seized the ship and killed the captain and the cook; the National Archives gives 1 July, and the National Park Service timeline says they revolted 'around 4:00am' on 2 July. In August 1839 Lt. Richard W. Mead of the USS Washington seized the Amistad off Long Island.
c-us3-court-revolt.label: consensus

c-us3-court-vanburen.text: President Van Buren was in favor of extraditing the Africans to Cuba; before the Supreme Court they were represented by the former president John Quincy Adams.
c-us3-court-vanburen.label: consensus

c-us3-court-amistad-ruling.text: On 9 March 1841 Justice Joseph Story delivered the Court's decision: 'The negroes were never the lawful slaves of Ruiz or Montez, or of any other Spanish subject.' They were 'natives of Africa, and were kidnapped there, and were unlawfully transported to Cuba in violation of the laws and treaties of Spain', and so 'by the laws of Spain itself, were entitled to their freedom.'
c-us3-court-amistad-ruling.label: consensus

c-us3-court-return.text: In November 1841 thirty-five survivors sailed from New York for Africa aboard the barque Gentleman, reaching Sierra Leone in January 1842. The Amistad Committee (Tappan, Jocelyn and Leavitt) went on to found the Mende Mission 'to expand Christianity in Africa'.
c-us3-court-return.label: consensus

c-us3-sect-tallmadge.text: In 1819 the Tallmadge amendment called for 'the gradual extinction of slavery in Missouri'; the House passed its bill with the amendment and the Senate refused it.
c-us3-sect-tallmadge.label: consensus

c-us3-sect-missouri.text: The Missouri Compromise 'allowed Maine to enter the Union as a free state' and let Missouri enter 'any way it chose'; its Missouri act, 'APPROVED, March 6, 1820', outlawed slavery above the 36°30' line in the remainder of the Louisiana Territory. It stood until the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and in 1857 the Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional.
c-us3-sect-missouri.label: consensus

c-us3-sect-firebell.text: On 22 April 1820 Thomas Jefferson wrote to John Holmes that 'this momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror', and that 'we have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go.'
c-us3-sect-firebell.label: consensus

c-us3-sect-gag.text: In 1836 a resolution introduced by Henry Laurens Pinckney of South Carolina provided that antislavery petitions be tabled without consideration. The House renewed the gag, and its version of December 1837 began: 'Resolved, that all petitions, memorials, and papers touching the abolition of slavery'.
c-us3-sect-gag.label: consensus

c-us3-sect-gag-repeal.text: John Quincy Adams led an eight-year struggle against the gag rule, as an infringement of the First Amendment right of petition; in 1837 he presented a petition from 22 slaves for emancipation. In 1844 his motion to repeal the standing 21st rule of the House carried by 108 votes to 80.
c-us3-sect-gag-repeal.label: consensus

c-us3-sect-wilmot.text: On 8 August 1846 David Wilmot, a Democratic congressman from Pennsylvania, moved to add to Polk's $2 million appropriation a proviso that 'as an express and fundamental condition to the acquisition of any territory from the Republic of Mexico' slavery should be prohibited there. The House passed it in a vote that split almost entirely along sectional lines; the Senate took it up the next day, but no vote was taken. In February 1847 the House passed it again, but the Senate passed the bill without it, and the House then accepted that version.
c-us3-sect-wilmot.label: consensus

c-us3-sect-wilmot-later.text: The Wilmot Proviso was never passed by both houses of Congress, but the Republican Party, founded in 1854, later supported the Wilmot principle.
c-us3-sect-wilmot-later.label: consensus

c-us3-sect-1848.text: In 1848 the Democrat Lewis Cass supported popular sovereignty, under which each territory would decide whether slavery was legal. A Free Soil convention at Buffalo on 9 August 1848 nominated Martin Van Buren on a platform of 'no more Slave States and no more Slave Territory' and 'Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor, and Free Men'; Frederick Douglass endorsed him. Zachary Taylor won the election, and Van Buren took 10 percent of the popular vote.
c-us3-sect-1848.label: consensus

pages.title: The young republic
pages.lede: Between the first census in 1790 and the census of 1850 the population of the United States rose from about 3.9 million to 23.2 million, and the number of states from 13 to 30. In the same years the first political parties formed, and the Louisiana Purchase doubled the country's size. This chapter follows that growth and those quarrels through sources from the census to Tocqueville.
body: The Constitution required an 'actual Enumeration' within three years of Congress's first meeting and every ten years after (US2.1); the Census Bureau's own history speaks of 'an almost immediate need for a census of the entire Nation'. [[c-us3-ov-enumeration]] The first count, in 1790, found 3,929,214 residents in 13 states, about 4.5 to the square mile, gathered by an estimated 650 enumerators; the Bureau lists Thomas Jefferson as the official in charge. [[c-us3-ov-1790]] Every later census found more people (see the chart), [[c-us3-ov-decades]] [[c-us3-ov-1830]] and by 1850 the count stood at 23,191,876 in 30 states, with New York City, at 515,547, the largest urban place. [[c-us3-ov-1850]]

Population grew nearly sixfold, but density did not even double, because the country itself grew: the census figures imply a land area of roughly 873,000 square miles in 1790 and about 2.94 million in 1850. [[c-us3-ov-area]] In 1803 the Louisiana Purchase, at roughly 4 cents an acre, doubled the size of the United States (US3.3). [[c-us3-ov-louisiana]]

Politics divided early. The French Revolution deepened existing divisions: Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson led the pro-French Democratic-Republicans, and Alexander Hamilton the Federalists, who viewed the Revolution with skepticism. [[c-us3-ov-parties]] The next pages follow Hamilton's programme (US3.1), the first party system (US3.2), Jefferson's presidency and the War of 1812 (US3.3), and religion and reform (US3.4); later pages turn to the market revolution, slavery, Jackson and the second party system, removal, Latin America, and the war with Mexico.

The evidence has its own pitfalls. The Annals of Congress, the record of debates from 1789 to 1824, were compiled between 1834 and 1856, mainly from newspaper accounts, and their speeches 'are paraphrased rather than presented verbatim'. [[c-us3-ov-annals]] Letters can be more direct: in 1791 Benjamin Banneker, a free Black American, wrote to Jefferson charging him with 'detaining by fraud and violence so numerous a part of my brethren under groaning captivity and cruel oppression'. [[c-us3-ov-banneker]] Alexis de Tocqueville's Democracy in America (1835 and 1840) asked how liberty could be preserved amid rising equality; 'nothing struck me more forcibly', he wrote, 'than the general equality of conditions'. [[c-us3-ov-tocqueville]]

pages.title: Washington and Hamilton
pages.lede: In 1790 Alexander Hamilton reported on the debts left by the Revolution and urged the Union to assume the states' debts; in 1791 Congress chartered a national bank, and Hamilton argued for government aid to manufactures. The bank divided Jefferson and Hamilton over how to read the Constitution, a federal whiskey tax met armed resistance in western Pennsylvania, and in 1796 Washington warned the nation against the spirit of party.
body: In January 1790 Hamilton reported that the federal debt, foreign and domestic, came to '54,124,464 dollars, and 56 cents', and that for the states' debts 'the total amount may be safely stated at 25 millions of dollars'. [[c-us3-ham-debt]] The debt, he wrote, 'was the price of liberty', and he concluded that 'it is expedient, there should be an assumption of the state debts by the Union.' [[c-us3-ham-assume]] How assumption passed is told in Jefferson's own later account, which the editors of his papers date '[1792?]'. He writes that he invited Hamilton and Madison to dinner ('I immediately wrote to each to come and dine with me the next day'), and that 'It ended in Mr. Madison's acquiescence in a proposition that the question should be again brought before the house': Madison would not vote for assumption but 'should not be strenuous' against it, two members whose districts lay on the Potomac, White and Lee, would change their votes, and the capital would move to the Potomac, with 'an intermediate residence at Philadelphia' to win Pennsylvania. [[c-us3-ham-bargain]]

Washington signed the bill for a Bank of the United States in February 1791. It had $10 million in capital, $2 million of it owned by the government, and opened in Philadelphia on 12 December 1791 with a twenty-year charter. [[c-us3-ham-bank]] Jefferson and Hamilton disagreed over it. Jefferson argued that 'the constitution allows only the means which are "necessary" not those which are merely "convenient"'; Hamilton answered that 'necessary often means no more than needful, requisite, incidental, useful, or conducive to.' [[c-us3-ham-necessary]] (For the Supreme Court's later answer, see US2.2.) When the charter came up for renewal in 1811, the House rejected it by one vote, and Vice President George Clinton broke a tie in the Senate against it. [[c-us3-ham-bank-1811]]

Hamilton's Report on Manufactures of 5 December 1791 argued that for new industries 'the interference and aid of their own government are indispensible' (his spelling). [[c-us3-ham-manuf]] The whiskey excise of 1791, the first national internal revenue tax, met armed resistance: in July 1794 about 500 armed men burned the home of the regional tax inspector, Washington sent some 13,000 troops into western Pennsylvania, 'the opposition melted away', and the two men convicted of treason were later pardoned. [[c-us3-ham-whiskey]] In his Farewell Address of 19 September 1796 Washington warned of 'the baneful effects of the Spirit of Party', advised the nation 'to steer clear of permanent Alliances', and wrote that 'Religion and morality are indispensable supports.' [[c-us3-ham-farewell]]

Economists still weigh Hamilton's system. Peter Rousseau and Richard Sylla argue that the financial system built in the 1790s 'was central to the nation's early growth and modernization', and a 2021 study by Hall, Payne, Sargent and Szőke measures how long Hamilton's policy took to work 'by building a reputation for servicing debts as promised'. Historians also stress what the founding era cost ordinary people: Terry Bouton's Taming Democracy (2007), a study of Pennsylvania, argues, in a reviewer's words, that the American gentry from 1776 to roughly 1800 succeeded at 'stunting the meaning and practice of democracy for ordinary white men.' [[c-us3-ham-legacy]]

pages.title: The first party system
pages.lede: Jefferson and Hamilton had already clashed over the Bank (US3.1). The French Revolution 'exacerbated pre-existing political divisions' and aligned the political elite along pro-French and pro-British lines, behind Hamilton's Federalists and Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans. A Federalist Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts in 1798, Jefferson and Madison, keeping their authorship secret, answered with the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, and the tied election of 1800 led to the Twelfth Amendment.
body: The French Revolution deepened existing divisions in American politics. Jefferson led the pro-French Democratic-Republicans, and Hamilton the Federalists, who viewed the Revolution with skepticism. [[c-us3-party-france]] John Jay's treaty with Britain was 'immensely unpopular with the American public', but it 'squeaked through the Senate on a 20 to 10 vote on June 24, 1795.' [[c-us3-party-jay]]

In 1798 a Federalist-controlled Congress passed four laws known together as the Alien and Sedition Acts. They raised the residency requirement for citizenship from 5 to 14 years, and the Sedition Act made it a crime to publish any 'false, scandalous, and malicious writing' about the government. The only journalists prosecuted under it were editors of Democratic-Republican newspapers. [[c-us3-party-acts]] The Sedition Act was to last 'until the third day of March, one thousand eight hundred and one, and no longer.' [[c-us3-party-sunset]]

Jefferson and Madison drafted the reply, and kept their authorship secret because they feared arrest for sedition. Their resolutions treated the Union as 'a compact among individual states'; Kentucky passed Jefferson's in 1798, and Virginia its 'more temperate resolution' on Christmas Eve. [[c-us3-party-authors]] Virginia's declared that the states 'have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose'. [[c-us3-party-va]] A further Kentucky resolution, of December 1799, declared that 'a nullification, by those sovereignties, of all unauthorized acts done under colour of that instrument, is the rightful remedy'. [[c-us3-party-ky]] What these words meant is still argued. In the early 1830s John Calhoun and Robert Hayne cited the resolutions as precedents for nullification; Madison denied that a single state could nullify federal law within its borders (US3.7). [[c-us3-party-later]]

In 1800 Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied in the electoral college, because electors could not say which of their votes was for president. The House chose Jefferson on 17 February 1801, after 36 ballots, and Hamilton tried to 'engineer support for Jefferson' over Burr. [[c-us3-party-1800]] The Twelfth Amendment, ratified on 15 June 1804, requires electors to vote for the vice president 'in distinct ballots'. [[c-us3-party-12th]] Jefferson later called his election 'as real a revolution in the principles of our government as that of 76.' [[c-us3-party-roane]]

pages.title: Jefferson's republic
pages.lede: In 1803 the United States bought Louisiana from France for $15 million, though Jefferson doubted that the Constitution allowed it, and Lewis and Clark crossed the continent to the Pacific. The embargo of 1807-09 cost about 8 percent of GNP by Douglas Irwin's estimate, the war with Britain that began in 1812 ended in a peace that restored the prewar boundaries, and the Hartford Convention helped bring down the Federalist Party.
body: Napoleon gave up his plans for Louisiana when his army in St. Domingue 'was being decimated by yellow fever, and war between France and England still threatened'. [[c-us3-jeff-napoleon]] Jefferson had sent James Monroe to join Robert Livingston in France, and in 1803 the United States bought Louisiana, about 828,000 square miles, for $15 million, [[c-us3-jeff-purchase]] roughly 4 cents an acre, doubling the country's size. [[c-us3-ov-louisiana]] Jefferson wrote to John Breckinridge that 'the constitution has made no provision for our holding foreign territory', and that the Executive had 'done an act beyond the constitution.' [[c-us3-jeff-constitution]] Robert J. Miller argues, in his publisher's summary, that Jefferson used the Doctrine of Discovery 'to exert American authority in the Louisiana Territory' and to 'conquer' the Indian nations; the official histories describe a purchase of territory from France. [[c-us3-jeff-miller]]

On 14 May 1804 William Clark and the Corps of Discovery, more than 45 strong, left Camp River Dubois. They reached the Pacific by November 1805 and were back in St. Louis on 23 September 1806. Among them were Sacagawea, the Shoshone wife of the interpreter Toussaint Charbonneau, with her newborn son, and York, 'who had been enslaved by William Clark since his childhood.' [[c-us3-jeff-corps]]

From December 1807 to March 1809 the United States imposed an embargo on its own international shipping. Douglas Irwin estimates its cost at about 8 percent of 1807 GNP, when trade was roughly 13 percent of output: some trade continued, and 'domestic producers successfully shifted production toward previously imported manufactured goods'. [[c-us3-jeff-embargo]] On 1 June 1812 Madison asked Congress to declare war on Great Britain. The causes included British impressment of American seamen and restrictions on neutral trade, but also 'western expansion, relations with American Indians, and territorial control of North America.' [[c-us3-jeff-war]] By 1814 neither side could claim a clear victory; the British blockaded the east coast and burned the White House and other government buildings in Washington. On Christmas Eve 1814 the Treaty of Ghent restored the 'status quo ante bellum'. [[c-us3-jeff-ghent]]

Federalists from five New England states met at Hartford from 15 December 1814 to 5 January 1815. Some raised the possibility of secession; the convention instead proposed amendments: to apportion representatives and direct taxes by 'free persons', to require two-thirds of both Houses to declare war unless the country was 'actually invaded', to limit embargoes to sixty days, and to bar a president 'from the same State two terms in succession'. [[c-us3-jeff-hartford]] Counting free persons alone would have ended the Constitution's count of 'three fifths of all other Persons' (US2.1). [[c-us3-jeff-threefifths]] Even as the convention finished, a British ship was still crossing the Atlantic with the terms of the Treaty of Ghent. As its emissaries approached Washington they 'were met by the news of Gen. Andrew Jackson's unexpected victory in the Battle of New Orleans', and 'its unpopularity was a factor in the demise of the Federalist Party.' [[c-us3-jeff-hartford-end]]
