pages.title: Religion and reform
pages.lede: The First Amendment bound Congress, but some states still kept established churches: Virginia guaranteed religious freedom by statute in 1786, and Massachusetts was the last of the original states to disestablish, in 1833. Revivals spread through the Methodist and Baptist churches and fed reforms from temperance to women's rights, while new movements such as the Latter-day Saints appeared beside older communities such as the Jews of Newport.
body: Virginia's Statute for Religious Freedom, written by Jefferson in 1777, was adopted on 16 January 1786, after James Madison's anonymous Memorial and Remonstrance opposed a General Assessment, a tax to support all Christian sects that Patrick Henry had championed. It provides that 'no man shall be compelled to frequent or support any religious worship, place, or ministry whatsoever.' [[c-us3-relig-virginia]] The First Amendment's words, 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion', named Congress (US2.9), [[c-us3-relig-first]] and Massachusetts was the last of the original 13 states to disestablish its churches, in 1833. [[c-us3-relig-mass]]

On 1 January 1802 Jefferson answered the Baptists of Danbury, Connecticut, with a phrase about 'a wall of separation between Church & State.' [[c-us3-relig-danbury]] In 1998 the FBI made his erased draft legible. It shows that on Levi Lincoln's advice he cut a section on fasts and thanksgivings, which Lincoln feared would hurt him among New England Republicans; Federalist preachers had used such days to revile Jefferson. James Hutson of the Library of Congress concludes that 'it was meant to be a political manifesto, nothing more', whereas the Supreme Court in Reynolds v. United States (1878) said Jefferson's words might be accepted 'almost as an authoritative declaration of the scope and effect of the [first] amendment'. [[c-us3-relig-hutson]]

The Second Great Awakening, roughly 1795 to 1835, grew 'particularly among Methodist and Baptist churches' and 'stimulated several moral and philanthropic reforms, including temperance and the emancipation of women.' [[c-us3-relig-awakening]] Crowd estimates for the camp meeting at Cane Ridge, Kentucky, in August 1801 'range from 10,000 to 30,000.' [[c-us3-relig-caneridge]] In Philadelphia, where 'blacks had been confined to the gallery' of St. George's church, Richard Allen and more than forty others left St. George's, and in 1816 Allen was consecrated bishop of the new African Methodist Episcopal Church. [[c-us3-relig-ame]] In one influential interpretation, Nathan Hatch argues that in these years 'American Christianity was democratized and common people became powerful actors on the religious scene.' [[c-us3-relig-hatch]] Latter-day Saints hold that an angel, Moroni, told Joseph Smith of engraved golden plates; [[c-us3-relig-moroni]] the Book of Mormon appeared in 1830, the church was organized on 6 April 1830, at Fayette or Manchester, New York (firsthand accounts by those present disagree), and Smith was killed by a mob at Carthage, Illinois, in 1844. [[c-us3-relig-lds]]

Newport's synagogue, dedicated in 1763, is the oldest synagogue building in the United States. [[c-us3-relig-touro]] In 1790 Washington wrote to its congregation that 'It is now no more that toleration is spoken of', praised a government 'which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance', and used the words 'every one shall sit in safety under his own vine and figtree, and there shall be none to make him afraid.' [[c-us3-relig-newport]] They closely follow Micah 4:4: 'they shall all sit under their own vines and under their own fig trees, and no one shall make them afraid'. [[c-us3-relig-micah]] The Jewish population, about 3,000 in 1820, 'ballooned from 15,000 to 150,000' between 1840 and 1860. [[c-us3-relig-jews]] The earliest temperance societies seem to have been those founded at Saratoga, New York, in 1808 and in Massachusetts in 1813; by 1833 there were 6,000 local societies. [[c-us3-relig-temperance]] At Seneca Falls on 19-20 July 1848, 68 women and 32 men signed a Declaration of Sentiments, drafted by Elizabeth Cady Stanton and the M'Clintock family, which held that 'all men and women are created equal'; eleven resolutions passed unanimously, but the suffrage resolution was only 'narrowly approved', after Frederick Douglass 'stood with Stanton' for it. [[c-us3-relig-seneca]]

pages.title: The market revolution
pages.lede: From Fulton's steamboat of 1807 to some 30,000 miles of railroad track by 1860, Americans built new ways to move goods, and the Erie Canal cut freight rates from upstate New York to the Atlantic by about 90 percent. Mills at Lowell spun cotton picked by enslaved people, and a Second Bank of the United States first fed and then tightened the credit boom that ended in the Panic of 1819. Historians still disagree over whether to call these changes a 'market revolution'.
body: Robert Fulton's steamboat ran 150 miles up the Hudson from New York to Albany in August 1807, a trip of 32 hours. [[c-us3-mkt-fulton]] Ten years later work began on the Erie Canal, which was completed in 1825; it ran 363 miles, and New York State authorized $7 million in loans to build it. [[c-us3-mkt-erie]] By the round figures of the historian Justin Nordstrom, freight rates from upstate New York to the Atlantic then fell by about 90 percent, and hauling time from 30 days to 10. [[c-us3-mkt-erie-freight]] About 3,000 miles of railroad track had been laid by 1840, and about 30,000 by 1860. [[c-us3-mkt-rail]] George Rogers Taylor called the years 1815 to 1860 'the transportation revolution' in the title of his book of 1951, and a retrospective a quarter-century later made 'the case for the permanent impact' of the book. [[c-us3-mkt-taylor]]

The Merrimack Manufacturing Company, incorporated in 1822, produced its first textiles in 1823 as the first mill in what became Lowell; it was funded and planned by the Boston Associates, a group of Boston financiers who incorporated the town of Lowell in 1826 (on the Industrial Revolution in Britain, see 14.6). Lowell had 18,000 people by 1836 and 30,000 by 1850, and its cotton came from the South, 'picked and processed by enslaved men and women'. [[c-us3-mkt-lowell]] Its mill women walked out twice: in 1834, when 800 of them left work against a 12.5 percent wage cut, and in 1836, when between 1,500 and 2,000 workers turned out. [[c-us3-mkt-strikes]] Lowell National Historical Park, citing Edward Baptist, now says that the Merrimack company's cotton 'took slaves a combined 100,000 days of labor per year to produce' (US3.6). [[c-us3-mkt-lowell-slavery]]

Credit expanded too. Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States in April 1816 with $35 million in capital, and it opened in January 1817 (for its constitutionality, McCulloch v. Maryland, see US2.2). [[c-us3-mkt-bank2]] Three economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, James Narron, David Skeie and Donald Morgan, tell the story of what followed: farmers and speculators bid up land on easy credit from state banks, which the Second Bank did little to restrain and even fed in its western branches; then cotton prices 'plummeted in January 1819 after British investors substituted to Indian cotton', and the Bank's deflationary tightening brought down prices and land values. Federal Reserve History calls the result 'a financial panic that drove the economy into a steep recession'. [[c-us3-mkt-1819]]

Was all this a 'market revolution'? Charles Sellers, in The Market Revolution (1991), his most widely debated book, described a shift 'from an agrarian to a capitalist society' that carried real costs. [[c-us3-mkt-sellers]] Daniel Walker Howe, in What Hath God Wrought (2007), dates the change earlier, judges it less harmful and argues that 'most American family farmers welcomed the chance to buy and sell in larger markets'; he refuses the term and writes of a 'communications revolution' instead. [[c-us3-mkt-howe]] Daniel Feller warned that 'a monograph that presupposes a market revolution will certainly discover one'. [[c-us3-mkt-feller]]

pages.title: Slavery and the cotton South
pages.lede: Congress banned the import of enslaved people from 1808, but slavery and the trade within the country went on: between the Constitution and the Civil War about a million people were moved from the Upper South to the Lower South, and cotton output rose from about 3,000 bales in 1790 to about 2 million a year by the mid-1840s. Historians and economic historians disagree sharply over how slavery and capitalism were linked. Virginia tightened its laws after Nat Turner's revolt of 1831, the year in which William Lloyd Garrison launched The Liberator.
body: Jefferson signed the act banning the import of enslaved people on 2 March 1807 (for the Constitution's 1808 clause, see US1.12). It took effect on 1 January 1808 and imposed heavy penalties on international traders, but it did not end slavery itself or the domestic sale of enslaved people, though it required manifests for those shipped along the coast. [[c-us3-slav-1808]] As Henry Louis Gates Jr. reports, drawing on the historian Walter Johnson, in the seven decades between the ratification of the Constitution and the Civil War about one million enslaved people were moved from the Upper South to the Lower South, roughly two-thirds of them through the domestic slave trade. [[c-us3-slav-domestic]]

Cotton output rose from 3,135 bales in 1790 to 731,452 in 1830 by L. C. Gray's figures, and by Fogel and Engerman's rounded figures to about 2 million a year by the mid-1840s and about 4 million on the eve of the Civil War. [[c-us3-slav-cotton]] Edward Baptist, in The Half Has Never Been Told (2014), argues that violence drove the rise in productivity: as Eric Foner summarises him, 'Violence, Baptist contends, explains the remarkable increase of labor productivity'. [[c-us3-slav-baptist]] Sven Beckert's idea of 'war capitalism' holds, in a University of Cape Town report of 2014, that early capitalism 'depended not on free wage labour, but on slavery and other unfree forms of labour'. [[c-us3-slav-beckert]] The economic historians Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode reply that Baptist, Beckert and Walter Johnson 'mishandle historical evidence and mis-characterize important events' (2018); their own research found that picking rates 'increased about fourfold between 1801 and 1862', driven by 'new cotton varieties' (2008). [[c-us3-slav-olmstead]] Northern mills such as Lowell's drew on this cotton (US3.5). [[c-us3-mkt-lowell-slavery]]

On the night of 21-22 August 1831, in Southampton County, Virginia, Nat Turner's rebels killed 'fifty-five white men, women, and children'. White people then killed 'roughly three dozen Black people without trials', and Turner was executed on 11 November. [[c-us3-slav-turner]] The Virginia legislature judged ending slavery 'inexpedient' and passed restrictions 'aimed at further suppressing Black religion and limiting the rights of free Blacks'. [[c-us3-slav-virginia]]

In Philadelphia, Richard Allen had built Bethel church, and in 1816 he 'united other African Methodist congregations' into the African Methodist Episcopal Church and became its bishop. [[c-us3-slav-allen]] On 1 January 1831 William Lloyd Garrison began The Liberator, promising that he would 'not equivocate', would 'not retreat a single inch' and would 'be heard'. [[c-us3-slav-garrison]] Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery on 3 September 1838, 'dressed as a sailor', and in 1845 published his first autobiography. [[c-us3-slav-douglass]]

pages.title: Jackson's democracy
pages.lede: Most states reduced or dropped property tests for voting, and turnout among those entitled to vote, by the American Presidency Project's figures, rose from 57.6 percent in 1828 to 80.2 percent in 1840, but New York and Pennsylvania shut most Black men out. Andrew Jackson won the presidency in 1828, vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank, and ended South Carolina's nullification of the tariff with a Compromise Tariff and a Force Bill. His opponents organised as the Whigs, and historians still disagree over what his democracy meant.
body: 'Suffrage was expanded as property and other restrictions on voting were reduced or abandoned in most states,' in Britannica's summary. [[c-us3-jack-suffrage]] The gain was for white men. New York's constitution of 1821 dropped the property test for white men but required 'm[e]n of colour' to own a freehold worth $250; in 1825 only 298 of nearly 6,000 free adult Black New Yorkers qualified. [[c-us3-jack-ny1821]] In 1838 Pennsylvania restricted the vote 'to "white freemen" only'. [[c-us3-jack-pa1838]] By the American Presidency Project's figures, which before 1920 are 'adjusted for the shifting definition of citizens with voting rights' (women, for example, are excluded), turnout among those entitled to vote rose from 57.6 percent in 1828 to 80.2 percent in 1840. [[c-us3-jack-turnout]]

In 1828 Jackson beat John Quincy Adams by 642,553 popular votes (56 percent) to 500,897 (43.6 percent), and by 178 electoral votes to 83; in South Carolina and Delaware the legislatures chose the electors. [[c-us3-jack-1828]] Vetoing the Bank's recharter on 10 July 1832, he wrote: 'It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes.' [[c-us3-jack-veto]] In 1833 he ordered the federal deposits removed from the Bank, and its federal charter ended in 1836. [[c-us3-jack-deposits]] What caused the Panic of 1837 is debated. Peter Temin (1969) argued that the boom before it 'did not have its origins in the Bank Wars' and pointed to Mexican silver and 'the money-tightening policies of the Bank of England'; Peter Rousseau (2002) blames the Treasury's transfers of government balances between banks and 'a policy-induced increase in the demand for coin in the Western states'. [[c-us3-jack-1837]]

On 24 November 1832 a South Carolina convention at Columbia declared the tariffs of 1828 and 1832 'null, void, and no law, nor binding upon this State, its officers or citizens'. Jackson's proclamation of 10 December replied that 'disunion, by armed force, is TREASON'. [[c-us3-jack-nullify]] On 2 March 1833 he signed both a Compromise Tariff and a Force Bill; South Carolina then rescinded its nullification of the tariffs and nullified the Force Bill instead. [[c-us3-jack-compromise]] Jackson's opponents 'formally organized' the Whig party in 1834 against 'King Andrew'. They favoured 'a protective tariff and federally financed internal improvements', and in 1840 they elected William Henry Harrison. [[c-us3-jack-whigs]]

Historians have judged Jacksonian democracy in very different ways. Arthur Schlesinger Jr. (1945) saw an effort to 'control the power of the capitalist groups'; Edward Pessen saw democratic rhetoric that hid inequality; Robert Remini called Jackson a genuine 'man of the people'; Daniel Walker Howe calls the Jacksonians champions of white male supremacy. [[c-us3-jack-legacy]] Daniel Feller notes that Schlesinger gave Indian affairs two sentences: 'Indian removal simply didn't seem that important to [Schlesinger]' (US3.8). [[c-us3-jack-feller]]

pages.title: Native nations and removal
pages.lede: Under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, Jackson's government signed almost 70 removal treaties and relocated nearly 50,000 people to Indian Territory, by the National Archives' count. The Supreme Court held in 1832 that Georgia's laws had no force in the Cherokee nation, yet after a minority faction signed a treaty more than 16,000 Cherokee were forcibly evicted in 1838-39, and at least a thousand died. The Seminoles fought removal in Florida, and historians still disagree over how to judge it.
body: Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act on 28 May 1830. It 'authorized the President to negotiate removal treaties with Indian tribes living east of the Mississippi River'. [[c-us3-remov-act]] In his message to Congress of 6 December 1830 he presented removal as part of 'the benevolent policy of the Government'. [[c-us3-remov-message]] By the end of his presidency, the National Archives counts, almost 70 removal treaties had been signed, nearly 50,000 eastern Indians had been relocated to Indian Territory, and 25 million acres had been opened to white settlement. [[c-us3-remov-totals]]

The Cherokee defended their land with their own laws. In 1829 Womankiller supported the death penalty for unauthorised sales of Cherokee land: 'It is a good law -- it will not kill the innocent but the guilty.' [[c-us3-remov-womankiller]] On 3 March 1832, in Worcester v. Georgia, Chief Justice Marshall wrote that 'The Cherokee nation, then, is a distinct community occupying its own territory, with boundaries accurately described, in which the laws of Georgia can have no force'. [[c-us3-remov-worcester]] The retort often put in Jackson's mouth, beginning 'John Marshall has made his decision', is in Daniel Feller's judgement 'dubious at best'. [[c-us3-remov-quip]] In late 1835 a 'small, rump faction' signed the Treaty of New Echota, and the Senate ratified it in May 1836. [[c-us3-remov-echota]] That year Principal Chief John Ross told the Senate: 'Our cause is your own. It is the cause of liberty and justice.' [[c-us3-remov-ross]] Removal began in May 1838 and was completed by the end of March 1839: more than 16,000 Cherokee were forcibly evicted and sent to Indian Territory, in present-day Oklahoma. [[c-us3-remov-trail]]

How many died is uncertain. The National Park Service says more than a thousand Cherokee died on the journey and 'perhaps several thousand' more from its consequences; the National Archives says about 4,000 of 16,000 died; a 2017 blog post of the National Museum of the American Indian says that about a quarter of 'more than 20,000' died. [[c-us3-remov-deaths]] In Florida the Seminoles fought three wars, in 1817-18, 1835-42 and 1855-58. The first began over attempts to recapture 'runaway Black slaves living among Seminole bands'; the second followed most Seminoles' refusal to leave their reservation and, by the Seminole Nation Museum's account, began with 'Dade's Massacre in December 1835'. [[c-us3-remov-seminole]] Its cost is disputed: Britannica gives $40-60 million and up to 2,000 U.S. soldiers killed, the Seminole Nation Museum about $15 million and more than 1,500. By 1842 about 3,000 Seminoles had been removed; the museum counts about 3,500 Seminoles in Florida today, descended from those who stayed or returned. [[c-us3-remov-seminole-cost]]

How to judge removal is debated. Francis Paul Prucha (1969) rejected a 'devil theory': 'To call Jackson an Indian-hater... is to speak in terms that had little meaning to Jackson'; 'To Jackson this seemed the only answer.' [[c-us3-remov-prucha]] Claudio Saunt (2020) calls removal 'not an inevitable chapter' but 'a fiercely contested political act designed to secure new lands for the expansion of slavery', which deported '80,000 men, women and children'. [[c-us3-remov-saunt]] At the Society for Historians of the Early American Republic's 2020 plenary session, Daniel Feller dismissed the view that removal was 'deliberately vicious and inhuman, if not overtly genocidal'; in The Panorama, the society's blog, Jeffrey Ostler replied that the United States 'bears responsibility for this and other genocidal policies'. Theda Perdue and Michael Green call removal 'ethnic cleansing', and Gary Clayton Anderson, in Ostler's summary, argues that it was ethnic cleansing and explicitly not genocide. [[c-us3-remov-genocide]]

pages.title: The Monroe Doctrine and Latin America
pages.lede: In 1819 Spain ceded East and West Florida to the United States by treaty, and in 1822 President Monroe told Congress that the new American states ought to be recognised. In December 1823 he declared the Americas closed to future European colonisation, a principle the United States could enforce only in the late 1800s. The doctrine has been reread ever since, from the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 to a 'Trump Corollary' in 2025.
body: In 1818, in a raid against the Seminoles and escaped slaves (US3.8), Andrew Jackson 'seized the Spanish forts at Pensacola and St. Marks'. [[c-us3-monroe-florida]] The Adams-Onís, or Transcontinental, Treaty was signed at Washington on 22 February 1819. Its Article II reads: 'His Catholic Majesty cedes to the United States, in full property and sovereignty, all the territories which belong to him, situated to the eastward of the Mississippi, known by the name of East and West Florida.' [[c-us3-monroe-treaty]] The United States took on liability for '$5 million in damage done by American citizens who rebelled against Spain', Spain gave up its claims to the Pacific Northwest, the United States recognised Spanish sovereignty over Texas (US3.10), and the treaty was ratified in 1821. [[c-us3-monroe-florida]]

On 8 March 1822 Monroe told Congress that 'the Provinces which have declared their independence and are in the enjoyment of it ought to be recognized' (on the wars of independence, see 14.5). [[c-us3-monroe-1822]] In August 1823 the British foreign minister, George Canning, suggested a joint Anglo-American declaration, but Secretary of State John Quincy Adams 'vigorously opposed cooperation with Great Britain'. [[c-us3-monroe-canning]] In his message to Congress of 2 December 1823 Monroe declared that the American continents 'are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers', and that the United States would consider any attempt by the European powers 'to extend their system to any portion of this hemisphere as dangerous to our peace and safety'. He added: 'With the existing colonies or dependencies of any European power we have not interfered and shall not interfere.' [[c-us3-monroe-text]]

The Office of the Historian sums up the doctrine as 'separate spheres of influence for the Americas and Europe, non-colonization, and non-intervention', and notes that only 'In the late 1800s' did U.S. economic and military power enable it to enforce it. [[c-us3-monroe-canning]] Simón Bolívar distrusted the United States: in a letter of August 1829 to Colonel Patrick Campbell, the British chargé d'affaires, he wrote that it seemed 'destined to plague America with miseries in the name of Freedom'. [[c-us3-monroe-bolivar]]

Later readings changed the doctrine's meaning. The Roosevelt Corollary of 1904 envisioned the United States as 'an international police power', and the Office of the Historian says it 'inverted the original meaning of the doctrine'. [[c-us3-monroe-roosevelt]] The historian Jay Sexton, in Kirkus's summary of his argument, sees in the doctrine 'a fusion of anti-colonialism and interventionism'. [[c-us3-monroe-sexton]] On 18 November 2013 Secretary of State John Kerry told the Organization of American States: 'The era of the Monroe Doctrine is over.' [[c-us3-monroe-kerry]] The National Security Strategy released in early December 2025 states that the United States 'will reassert and enforce the Monroe Doctrine to restore American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere', under what it calls a 'Trump Corollary', which Global News reports prioritises American-led cooperative efforts against mass migration, drug trafficking and 'hostile foreign incursion or ownership of key assets'. [[c-us3-monroe-2025]] Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said: 'Past administrations perpetuated the belief that the Monroe Doctrine had expired. They were wrong'; the political scientist Max Cameron of the University of British Columbia said that recent U.S. military operations in the region had created 'a sense of horror in many places that this is a return to gunboat diplomacy'. [[c-us3-monroe-2025-views]]

pages.title: Texas and the war with Mexico
pages.lede: Texas broke away from Mexico in 1836 and joined the United States in 1845. A quarrel over its border led to war in 1846, and in 1848 Mexico ceded 55 percent of its territory. Americans such as Lincoln, Thoreau and Douglass opposed the war, and Mexican writers blamed it on American ambition.
body: Mexico's Law of April 6, 1830 tried to stop Anglo-American immigration into Texas and further imports of slaves, but in the Handbook of Texas's words it 'only slowed immigration and the Peculiar Institution, but did not curb them.' [[c-us3-mex-1830]] By 1834 the non-Indian population was about 21,000, by Almonte's estimate. [[c-us3-mex-pop1834]] The Handbook describes the centralist government of the Siete Leyes, which replaced the federal Constitution of 1824, and notes that slavery 'has also been cited as an underlying cause' of the revolt that followed, because of 'slaveowners' concern with protecting their peculiar institution'. [[c-us3-mex-causes]] Texas declared independence on 2 March 1836, under a constitution that guaranteed the protection of slavery, and the Alamo fell four days later. [[c-us3-mex-1836]] About 350 prisoners were killed at Goliad. At San Jacinto on 21 April a battle of eighteen minutes cost the Mexican army 630 dead and 730 captured. [[c-us3-mex-goliad-sj]] On slavery in the wider republic, see US3.6.

Annexation took nine more years. Congress passed the annexation resolution on 28 February 1845, and Texas legally entered the Union on 29 December; antislavery sentiment had been the chief obstacle. [[c-us3-mex-annex]] That summer an unsigned article in the Democratic Review, usually credited to its editor John L. O'Sullivan (Linda Hudson credits Jane McManus Storm Cazneau), spoke of 'our manifest destiny to overspread the continent allotted by Providence', and said of annexation: 'Slavery had nothing to do with it.' [[c-us3-mex-osullivan]] Historians read the phrase differently. In its publisher's summary, Reginald Horsman's Race and Manifest Destiny (1981) shows that 'the belief in white American superiority was firmly ensconced in the nation's ideology by 1850'; Frederick Merk (1963), in John Mack Faragher's words, 'rejected inevitability in favor of a more contingent interpretation of American expansionism in the 1840s'. [[c-us3-mex-manifest]] The appeal to Providence states the writer's faith; it is evidence of how expansionists spoke, not of what Providence intended. The immediate quarrel was the border. Mexico held that Texas ended at the Nueces River, the United States that it ran to the Rio Grande, and Slidell was sent to Mexico to negotiate the purchase of the disputed areas. [[c-us3-mex-border]] The first major battle was fought at Palo Alto on 8 May 1846, and the United States declared war on 13 May. [[c-us3-mex-war1846]]

Some Americans opposed the war. On 22 December 1847 Abraham Lincoln, in his Spot Resolutions, asked 'Whether the spot on which the blood of our citizens was shed, as in his messages declared,' was really American soil; the House never acted on them. [[c-us3-mex-spot]] Henry David Thoreau spent a night in jail rather than pay his poll tax to a government that, in Britannica's summary of his view, endorsed slavery and waged an imperialist war against Mexico, and his essay of 1849 came to be called 'Civil Disobedience'. [[c-us3-mex-thoreau]] Frederick Douglass wrote in The North Star: 'Slavery, treachery and mad ambition, are at the head of the government, in the person of James K. Polk'. [[c-us3-mex-douglass]] Historians still divide. Amy S. Greenberg presents a war waged against an unoffending neighbor, while Robert W. Merry judges that Polk fulfilled the vision of those who elected him. [[c-us3-mex-justwar]] Of 78,718 Americans who served, 1,733 died in battle and 11,550 died of other causes, more than six times as many. [[c-us3-mex-losses]]

The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848, made the Rio Grande the border. Mexico ceded 55 percent of its territory, more than 500,000 square miles, and the United States paid 'the sum of fifteen millions of dollars' and took over claims against Mexico up to 'three and one-quarter millions of dollars'. [[c-us3-mex-treaty]] [[c-us3-mex-area]] Mexicans in the ceded lands could stay or leave with their property. Those who stayed could 'retain the title and rights of Mexican citizens' by saying so within a year; the rest 'shall be incorporated into the Union of the United States', with full citizenship when Congress judged proper. [[c-us3-mex-citizens]] The Senate approved the treaty on 10 March 1848, by 38 votes to 14, but rewrote Article IX and deleted Article X, which guaranteed the protection of Mexican land grants. [[c-us3-mex-senate]] [[c-us3-mex-senate-vote]] Mexican writers, among them Alcaraz, Payno and Ramírez, concluded that 'the insatiable ambition of the United States, favored by our weakness, caused it.' [[c-us3-mex-otherside]] Mexicans call the conflict the Guerra de 1847 or the Guerra de Estados Unidos a México, and in Mexico 'the loss of battles and territories was a national trauma', followed by turmoil, civil war and foreign intervention. [[c-us3-mex-names]] Why Mexico lost is argued. Peter Guardino puts economics first, rather than disunity, while Brian DeLay points to years of raids by Native warriors that had left northern Mexico 'too divided, exhausted, and distracted to resist'. [[c-us3-mex-whylost]]

practice.q: Under the treaty as the Senate approved it, what was the position of Mexicans living in the ceded lands?
choices: Those declaring it within a year kept Mexican citizenship
They had to leave the ceded lands within a year of the treaty
Article X of the treaty guaranteed their Mexican land grants
They had to take U.S. citizenship at once or lose their property
practice.why: Under Articles VIII and IX, as the Senate rewrote Article IX, those who stayed could 'retain the title and rights of Mexican citizens' by declaring so within one year; the rest would be incorporated into the United States.

wrong.1: They could stay or leave; the one-year limit applied to the choice of citizenship.
wrong.2: The Senate deleted Article X.
wrong.3: They kept their property whether they stayed or left, and full citizenship came only when Congress judged proper.

pages.title: Immigration and the cities
pages.lede: Recorded immigration rose from about 129,000 in the 1820s to over 1.4 million in the 1840s, most of it from Ireland and Germany. Arrivals jumped after the Irish Famine began in 1845, the port cities grew, and nativists turned on Catholic newcomers. In January 1848 gold was found in California, where the Indian population collapsed in the decades that followed.
body: Recorded arrivals in the United States rose from 128,502 in the 1820s to 538,381 in the 1830s and 1,427,337 in the 1840s, and then to 2,814,554 in the 1850s. [[c-us3-immig-decades]] Ireland and Germany supplied about seven in ten of them: 656,145 Irish and 385,434 Germans in the 1840s, and 1,029,486 Irish and 976,072 Germans in the 1850s. [[c-us3-immig-origins]] [[c-us3-immig-decades]]

The Irish surge followed the potato blight. From 1845 late blight, Phytophthora infestans, caused the potato crop to fail, and the Great Famine lasted until 1849, or 1851 by some reckonings. [[c-us3-immig-blight]] About a million people died of starvation and disease, and over a million emigrated. [[c-us3-immig-famine-toll]] The American figures show the jump: 114,371 arrivals in 1845, 154,416 in 1846 and 234,968 in 1847, then 369,980 in 1850 and 427,833 in 1854. [[c-us3-immig-yearly]]

The cities grew fast. New York had 123,706 people in 1820, 312,710 in 1840 and 515,547 in 1850; Baltimore, Boston and New Orleans had all passed 100,000 by 1850, Cincinnati more than doubled in the 1840s, to 115,435, and St. Louis grew from 16,469 to 77,860. [[c-us3-immig-cities]] In Philadelphia in May and July 1844, Catholic objections to reading the Protestant King James Bible in the public schools led to 'some of the bloodiest rioting of the antebellum period', and rioters burned St. Michael's and St. Augustine's Catholic churches. [[c-us3-immig-phila]] In 1849 the secret Order of the Star-Spangled Banner formed in New York City; it grew into the anti-Catholic, anti-immigrant Know-Nothing movement, and by late 1855, 43 members of the House were avowed members. [[c-us3-immig-knownothing]] On religion in the young republic, see US3.4.

On 24 January 1848 James W. Marshall found flakes of gold at Sutter's sawmill on the South Fork of the American River, in the valley the Nisenan called Cullumah, 'beautiful valley'. [[c-us3-immig-gold]] Within a year about 80,000 'forty-niners' had arrived. [[c-us3-immig-49ers]] Between 1846 and 1873 California's Indian population fell from perhaps 150,000 to 30,000. [[c-us3-immig-calpop]] Benjamin Madley argues that the killing in these years was genocide; Newsweek reports his estimate that 'between 9,000 and 16,000 Indians, though probably many more, were killed'. Gary Clayton Anderson calls it ethnic cleansing, not genocide, and puts the number killed at no more than 2,000. [[c-us3-immig-genocide]] On the removal of Native nations in the East, see US3.8.

practice.q: Yearly arrivals in the United States rose from 114,371 in 1845 to 234,968 in 1847. Which explanation fits the evidence best?
choices: Famine after the blight of 1845 drove the Irish to emigrate
The discovery of gold in California drew migrants from abroad
The Know-Nothings recruited immigrant workers for the cities
German emigration stopped, leaving room for Irish workers
practice.why: Late blight caused the crop failures behind Ireland's Famine, from 1845, and over a million people left Ireland. Arrivals were already rising, but they jumped in 1846 and 1847; Ireland sent 656,145 people in the 1840s.

wrong.1: Gold was found only in January 1848, after the rise had begun.
wrong.2: The Know-Nothings' parent order was formed only in 1849, and the movement was anti-immigrant.
wrong.3: German arrivals rose too, from 124,726 in the 1830s to 385,434 in the 1840s.

practice.q: What lay behind Philadelphia's riots of 1844?
choices: Catholic objections to Protestant Bible reading in schools
The election victories of the Know-Nothings in the city
The arrival of thousands of refugees from the Irish Famine
Catholic attacks on Protestant churches in the city
practice.why: The riots grew out of Catholic objections to Protestant (King James) Bible reading in the public schools.

wrong.1: The order behind the Know-Nothings formed only in 1849, five years later.
wrong.2: The Famine began in 1845, the year after the riots.
wrong.3: The churches burned were Catholic: St. Michael's and St. Augustine's.

pages.title: The Supreme Court and the nation
pages.lede: Under John Marshall the Supreme Court protected corporate charters from the states and reaffirmed its power to review state courts. Roger Taney's Court read charters more narrowly. In the Amistad case of 1841 the Court freed Africans who had taken over the ship carrying them as slaves.
body: Marbury, McCulloch and Gibbons are treated as doctrine in US2.6 and US2.2; this page turns to other rulings. In Dartmouth College v. Woodward (1819) the Court held that the college's charter of 1769 was a contract, which New Hampshire could not alter, because the Constitution forbids states to impair the obligation of contracts. Marshall wrote that 'this is a contract the obligation of which cannot be impaired without violating the Constitution'. [[c-us3-court-dartmouth]] He also defined a corporation: 'A corporation is an artificial being, invisible, intangible, and existing only in contemplation of law.' [[c-us3-court-corporation]] Daniel Webster argued for the trustees, and the decision had far-reaching impact on business charters. [[c-us3-court-webster]] Two years later, in Cohens v. Virginia, the Court reaffirmed that it could review state-court judgments that raised federal questions, since 'a case arising under the Constitution or laws of the United States is cognizable in the Courts of the Union'. The opinion observed that 'In many States, the judges are dependent for office and for salary on the will of the legislature.' The Cohens themselves lost; their conviction stood. [[c-us3-court-cohens]]

Roger B. Taney succeeded Marshall as Chief Justice. In Charles River Bridge v. Warren Bridge, decided on 14 February 1837, the owners of a bridge chartered by Massachusetts in 1785 argued that their charter barred a rival bridge chartered in 1828. The Court disagreed. In the words of the case as printed in the United States Reports, 'in grants by the public, nothing passes by implication', and 'The object and the end of all Government is to promote the happiness and prosperity of the community'; and the same report adds that 'we must not forget, that the community also have rights'. [[c-us3-court-crb]] In the judgment of the Supreme Court Historical Society, Taney 'interpreted corporation charters more strictly, state powers more generously, than Marshall had.' [[c-us3-court-taney]] His reputation has been contested from the start. At his appointment a New York journal called him 'that political hack', while Edward Bates, Lincoln's Attorney General, hoped that his 'great error' in the Dred Scott case, which belongs to a later chapter, would not forever 'tarnish his otherwise well earned fame'. [[c-us3-court-taney-rep]]

Two Spanish planters, Pedro Montes and José Ruiz, bought 53 Africans and put them aboard the Cuban schooner Amistad. On the night of 1-2 July 1839 the Africans, led by Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué), seized the ship and killed the captain and the cook. In August the USS Washington took the Amistad off Long Island. [[c-us3-court-revolt]] President Van Buren favored extraditing the Africans to Cuba. Before the Supreme Court they were represented by the former president John Quincy Adams. [[c-us3-court-vanburen]] On 9 March 1841 Justice Joseph Story delivered the decision: 'The negroes were never the lawful slaves of Ruiz or Montez, or of any other Spanish subject.' They had been kidnapped in Africa and unlawfully transported to Cuba, and so 'by the laws of Spain itself, were entitled to their freedom.' [[c-us3-court-amistad-ruling]] In November 1841 thirty-five survivors sailed for Africa, reaching Sierra Leone in January 1842, and the Amistad Committee went on to found the Mende Mission 'to expand Christianity in Africa'. [[c-us3-court-return]] On slavery and the early abolitionists, see US3.6.

practice.q: How did Charles River Bridge (1837) differ from Dartmouth College (1819)?
choices: It read public grants narrowly: nothing passed by implication
It overruled Dartmouth and let states cancel charters at will
It denied that a corporation is 'an artificial being'
It held that the Supreme Court could not review state charters
practice.why: The 1785 charter did not, by implication, bar a rival bridge: 'in grants by the public, nothing passes by implication', and the community's rights weighed in the balance.

wrong.1: The Court read the 1785 charter narrowly; it did not cancel it, and Dartmouth's contract rule was not overruled.

practice.q: On what ground did the Supreme Court free the Amistad Africans in 1841?
choices: They were kidnapped Africans, free under Spain's own laws
Slavery itself was contrary to the U.S. Constitution
They had been born in Cuba and were protected by its laws
President Van Buren had asked the Court for their release
practice.why: Story found that they were 'natives of Africa' who had been 'kidnapped there', were never lawful slaves, and 'by the laws of Spain itself, were entitled to their freedom'.

wrong.1: The opinion rested on the laws and treaties of Spain, under which these kidnapped Africans were entitled to their freedom.
wrong.2: Story found they were natives of Africa, kidnapped there and unlawfully transported to Cuba.
wrong.3: Van Buren favored extraditing them to Cuba.

pages.title: The sectional crisis begins
pages.lede: In 1820 the Missouri Compromise drew a line across the Louisiana Territory between slavery and freedom. In the House a gag on antislavery petitions lasted from 1836 to 1844. The war with Mexico revived the question of slavery in new territory, and by 1848 the Wilmot Proviso, popular sovereignty and the Free Soil Party offered rival answers.
body: In 1819 the Tallmadge amendment called for 'the gradual extinction of slavery in Missouri'; the House passed it and the Senate refused it. [[c-us3-sect-tallmadge]] Under the compromise of 1820, whose Missouri act was approved on 6 March, Maine entered the Union as a free state and Missouri was allowed to enter with slavery, and slavery was outlawed above the 36°30' line in the remainder of the Louisiana Territory (US3.3). It stood until the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854, and in 1857 the Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional. [[c-us3-sect-missouri]] Thomas Jefferson wrote to John Holmes that 'this momentous question, like a fire bell in the night, awakened and filled me with terror', and added: 'we have the wolf by the ear, and we can neither hold him, nor safely let him go.' [[c-us3-sect-firebell]]

In 1836 a resolution introduced by Henry Laurens Pinckney of South Carolina provided that antislavery petitions be tabled without consideration. The House renewed the gag; its version of December 1837 began 'Resolved, that all petitions, memorials, and papers touching the abolition of slavery'. [[c-us3-sect-gag]] John Quincy Adams led an eight-year struggle against it, as an infringement of the First Amendment right of petition, and in 1837 he presented a petition from 22 slaves for emancipation. In 1844 his motion to repeal the standing rule carried by 108 votes to 80. [[c-us3-sect-gag-repeal]] On the abolitionists themselves, see US3.6.

The war with Mexico (US3.10) reopened the question of slavery in the territories. On 8 August 1846 David Wilmot, a Democratic congressman from Pennsylvania, moved to attach to Polk's $2 million appropriation a proviso that 'as an express and fundamental condition to the acquisition of any territory from the Republic of Mexico' slavery should be prohibited there. The House passed it in a vote that split almost entirely along sectional lines, but the Senate never voted on it. In February 1847 the House passed it again, but the Senate passed the bill without it, and the House then accepted that version. [[c-us3-sect-wilmot]] The proviso never passed both houses, but the Republican Party, founded in 1854, later took up its principle. [[c-us3-sect-wilmot-later]]

By 1848 the parties gave different answers. The Democrat Lewis Cass supported popular sovereignty, under which each territory would decide whether slavery was legal. A Free Soil convention at Buffalo on 9 August 1848 nominated Martin Van Buren on a platform of 'no more Slave States and no more Slave Territory' and 'Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor, and Free Men', and Frederick Douglass endorsed him. Zachary Taylor won the presidency, and Van Buren took 10 percent of the popular vote. [[c-us3-sect-1848]]

practice.q: Why did the 36°30' line of 1820 not settle whether slavery could spread into the lands won from Mexico?
choices: It covered only what remained of the Louisiana Territory
Congress had repealed it in 1845, when Texas was annexed
The Wilmot Proviso had already extended it to the Pacific
The Supreme Court had struck it down before the war began
practice.why: The compromise outlawed slavery above 36°30' in the remainder of the Louisiana Territory; the Mexican lands lay outside it, which is why the Wilmot Proviso was fought over in 1846-47.

wrong.1: It stood until the Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854.
wrong.2: The Proviso would have barred slavery from all territory taken from Mexico, and it never passed both houses.
wrong.3: The Supreme Court ruled it unconstitutional in 1857, nine years after the war ended.

practice.q: How did John Quincy Adams frame his campaign against the gag rule?
choices: As a defense of the First Amendment right of petition
As a demand for the immediate abolition of slavery
As enforcement of the Missouri Compromise line of 1820
As support for the Free Soil platform of Van Buren
practice.why: He fought the rule as an infringement of the right of petition, and repeal carried 108 to 80 in 1844.

wrong.1: The fight was over whether the House would receive petitions; the gag tabled them without consideration.
wrong.2: The Missouri Compromise concerned slavery in the Louisiana Territory, not House procedure.
wrong.3: The Free Soil platform was adopted in August 1848, four years after repeal.
